speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (for the Minister of State (International Trade)) moved
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: that Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill was before this House at report stage until last Friday when after seven days of report stage debate, a debate which did not involve the question of exports and the need for financing and assistance to our exports but involved the issue of parliamentary accountability, the Government to some extent saw some reason and consented to the amendments which are now part of the Bill as presented to the House at this stage. Briefly, Mr. Speaker, those amendments reduced the gross limit of the Bill from a demand for the right to deal with $62 billion to a demand for the right to deal with $44.5 billion, a $17.5 billion reduction in demand.
[DOT]	(ino)
Second, those amendments require an automatic reference of the Export Development Corporation's performance to standing committees of the House so that the committees will be able to review annually the performance of this corporation as it works to assist the exporters of our country.
Last, Mr. Speaker, perhaps the most dramatic amendment is the change in terms of the borrowing arrangement for the corporation. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that under the Bill presented to Parliament and under the previous Export Development Act, the corporation was entitled to borrow in relation to its authorized capital. That borrowing is now limited to ten times the paid-in capital and retained earnings of the corporation. That in itself is a very dramatic form of parliamentary accountability.
We are not quite sure what the retained earnings of the corporation are at this point, but the corporation can borrow approximately $7 billion because that would be approximately ten times its paid-in capital and retained earnings. That is a far cry from the automatic right to borrow $20 billion without
having the Government put any money into the corporation at all.
This has, therefore, been a dramatic action largely led by this Party to make sure that Parliament again would have control over the public purse and would have some element of control over the activities of the corporation. The result of the debate that we have engaged in over the past weeks is proof, Sir, that Parliament can work, proof that if Members of Parliament are prepared to demand that the Crown be accountable, the Crown can be forced to be accountable. I think that is a tribute to the House and, indeed, it is a tribute to the Government that it finally saw the wisdom of the statements made and positions taken by members of this Party in requiring accountability to Parliament.
There are serious problems with the Export Development Corporation. Those problems were, to some extent, referred to by the many speakers who spoke at report stage on the various amendments. Before we finish this debate which, by House order, should finish today, I think it is essential that those particular positions be put to the House again for the record so that the officials of the Export Development Corporation may know where we stand, what we would like done with the corporation and how we would like to see that corporation run to the benefit of the trade of Canada.
There were serious allegations made about the efficiency of the Export Development Corporation in a study done by the Economic Council of Canada. I want to refer to that study first because I think it made a number of references to how the corporation should work. The Economic Council of Canada made a number of recommendations, Sir. 1 would like to go over those recommendations very briefly with Members of the House so that we can come to some type of consensus and formulate some type of direction from the House to the corporation as to how the corporation might better promote the exports of the country.
At one time, Sir, the corporation was essentially an insurance corporation for an exporter with a receivable from a foreign country or receivables from purchasers or consignees of Canadian goods in foreign countries. That exporter would purchase from the Export Development Corporation insurance coverage to cover all his world-wide export contracts with various countries and consignees. The corporation's basic business interests remained in the insurance field until 1970. It was only after 1970 that the corporation moved into the field of lending money.
A lot of the discussion on this Bill has been about the lending function of the corporation. Perhaps the most impor-

September 27, 1983
Export Development Act
tant thing the corporation could be engaged in is the insurance field. The Economic Council of Canada dealt with that aspect and said that in its view the corporation should be more involved in the export credit reinsurance and the insurance aspect-in other words, it should get back to where it was before, insuring and reinsuring of exports so that when they give credit on the sale of goods and services they are going to wind up with accounts that are collectable. When goods are shipped to a foreign consignee first of all, it is very difficult to get them back; second, in many cases there is an opportunity to sue in a foreign court; and third, in the process the company's working capital requirements have to be financed. The sale of goods to a purchaser in a foreign country represents risks that are entirely different from those involved in selling goods domestically. It is for that reason that exporters and their bankers demand insurance coverage. We must have a more aggressive insurance and reinsurance coverage.
The Economic Council of Canada talks about developing private markets for insurance, and reinsurance of those private insurers, so that exporters get paid for their goods.
The corporation had better examine the references regarding insurance made by the Economic Council of Canada. I say that because many exporters come to me complaining that they cannot get along with the Export Development Corporation. They say it is too fussy, it does not check credits, it gives small coverage on insurance and it is hard to get along with. One company claimed that the Export Development Corporation is a waste of time and it deals with the American Credit Indemnity Company of New York where they can get insurance at one-third or one-fifth of the cost of the Export Development Corporation's coverage.
Reference was made to the sale of a food conveyor system for an airport in Singapore. Apparently the negotiations with the Export Development Corporation became so cumbersome that they placed the business with the American Credit Indemnity Company where the premium was less. They got the coverage and were paid without any problem. But where was the Export Development Corporation's insurance program? It was working in a very bureaucratic and backward fashion with an attitude that it was not appropriate to the development of the trade.
The Economic Council of Canada suggested that the corporation should withdraw bit by bit from the lending field because there seems to be a limited number of borrowers who get assistance, and almost always it is the same group. For example, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has borrowed about 25 per cent of the money the corporation has lent. Is this financing export or is it financing Atomic Energy of Canada Limited under another heading? I think it is the latter. If we are going to sell atomic reactors, perhaps the Government of Canada should finance the sales but let us recognize it for what it is: it is financing Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, not export sales. Therefore, to a large extent, one begins to wonder whether this is not an implicit subsidy to a relatively few number of corporations which are receiving a subsidy and which perhaps should be designated to them. If they need a
subsidy they should have the subsidy, but it should not be buried under the glowing cloak of export assistance when in fact it is corporate assistance to businesses which may or may not be entitled to receive assistance year after year just because of foreign sales.
We must look at what the cost to Canada is for these particular businesses which seem continually to rely on the Export Development Corporation somehow as their banker at low interest cost. That low interest cost is a huge subsidy to these corporations. It does not appear anywhere in the estimates. That is something which we as a nation must look at. This is the kind of thing which the corporation must look at. Is the Export Development Corporation here to finance exports, or is it here to be a source of credit to a limited few which have, for one reason or another, the right to access money at very significantly subsidized rates?
Further, the Economic Council of Canada looks at the question of subsidizing rates, a concessionary financing. There is no question that what we have to do is struggle with our trading partners, with other countries which are leading exporters, and get rid of this business of subsidizing interest rates. That is not a question of fair trade; that is a question of subsidized trade. When we are looking at our tariff policy and at our dumping arrangements, our other trade arrangements, we ought very carefully to examine those countries which give concessionary financing for goods purchased by Canadians from those foreign countries. That type of assistance is nontariff assistance and should be treated as a form of dumping, a form of subsidizing exports, the kind of thing which, if it is going to continue, will seriously mar international trade. We had better get tough about the matter. It does not do the foreign country in balance any good. It does not do us any good to do it. It is expensive for all of us. We ought to get tough with those who do it by treating the goods which they export to Canada in a fashion different from what they claim to be a fair market basis. We ought to treat them as being pariahs in world trade and penalize them accordingly.
We might well be better off, Sir, as the Economic Council says, when we have a situation where it is a question of exporting goods or of reducing the need for imports, to spend more of our money reducing the need for imports, because that is the other aspect of trade. It is all very well to buy and sell goods all over the world, but sometimes one is just as well off to sell fewer goods and make more of the things and do more of those things at home that one can do at home. I wonder about the airplane business, for example. Are we all that bright in financing airplanes at concessionary rates to foreign purchasers but not to Canadians? Are we all that bright in financing ships for export to foreign countries but not for Canadians? In effect, the Canadian goes offshore to buy his ship because he can get concessionary financing. We sell ships to a foreigner with concessionary financing but not to Canadians. Where are we getting lost? It is not too bright, Mr. Speaker, and it is about time the EDC and the Minister started looking at the situation and saying somewhere along
September 27, 1983

the line that we have to do the business like, bottom line type of thing.
A lot has been said about the New York subway deal whereby we supplied the best part of $1 billion in concessionary rates. Even today they are concessionary rates, Sir. When the loan was committed to the City of New York it represented a subsidy of between 6 per cent and 7 per cent, an enormous subsidy on a per annum basis. Today rates have fallen and it does not represent that kind of subsidy at all, but it still is a small subsidy. The loan was justified on the basis of creating employment, but 40 per cent of the employment is American. The loan was justified on the basis of the export of our technology, and so on, to that great market in New York. At the same time we have cities in Canada which need commuter service, subway cars and so on, so should we not be offering that kind of financial assistance to our own people before we offer it to those around the world? When do the people of the City of New York have the right to assistance from Canada before the people of Montreal, Toronto or Vancouver?
Or Yorkton.

My friend says Yorkton.
I would like to move, Mr. Speaker, to the question of other types of financing that we might look at. We have before the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs a reference with respect to foreign banks. You will know, Sir, that under the Bank Act we have allowed some 58 foreign banks to operate in Canada. The reason for this is that our banks, which were certainly not large in terms of foreign business 15 or 20 years ago, have now become quite dominant in some foreign markets. Indeed, they rank high in a list of international banks doing business around the world. What we have to look at is the extent to which we can use our own Canadian bank network to promote and finance our trade and the extent to which foreign banks operating in Canada can help us with financing our foreign trade. After all, one of the reasons for bringing in a foreign bank to the country, presumably, is to finance trade activities. By and large they are not there to look after the ordinary citizens' deposit or chequing accounts or that type of thing; they are interested in commercial activity, and what we ought to look at in licensing foreign banks is their willingness to assist in financing Canada's export trade.
During the debate a great deal was made of the efficiency of the operation itself. The corporation's executives have probably heard to the full the fact that in their last year's report they indicated they had 613 employees, approximately ten employees for every loan customers. The fact is that they made about 120 loan transactions but with only 62 separate customers. Therefore, that corporation had ten employees for every loan transaction.
Then one goes on to the insurance account and finds that it wrote about 900 new insurance policies. It has about 1,320
Export Development Act
insurance accounts, but it wrote 900 new insurance accounts, amounting to one and a half insurance accounts for every employee.
When one finds that the corporation has offices in Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, Halifax and, of course, here in Ottawa, one begins to wonder, in view of the size of the corporation and the kinds of things it is doing, why it needs all this help and all these offices. After all, if it is only involved in 900 new guarantee deals in a year and if it has only 62 customers to whom to lend money, why does it need over 600 employees? The answer is that it does not.
No reasonable person could ever suggest that the corporation is efficiently and effectively managed. I say that because of the straight statistics produced by the corporation. The corporation may say that it must be very careful when it gives a credit line to a foreign country, that it must check out the economy of the country and ensure that the credit is worth while, and that it is necessary to employ economists and so on.
1 ask why? We do have a Department of External Affairs. We do have embassies and consulates around the world. Surely we do not need a duplicate arrangement involving the Export Development Corporation.
I therefore say to Your Honour that there is a great deal of room for fat trimming in the corporation. It is my hope that with the promise of the Minister that his new board of directors, which will now total 15, will have a significant private majority, this directorship will be comprised of people who will not be yes men or yes women. I hope these people will take a hard-nosed look at the activities of the Corporation, its employees, its expenses such as travelling costs, and, if necessary, contract out some of the work of the corporation. Is there any reason the corporation's insurance should not be available in major insurance offices around the country? Is there any reason the banks of the country should not be directly capable of dealing with the Export Development Corporation on their own, placing the paper, receiving the guarantee, much the same as they do under the Small Businesses Loans Act, for example? There is no reason at all.
I say to Your Honour that a great deal of overhead being carried and a great deal of bureaucracy could easily be eliminated. I hope that the private sector appointees will very quickly turn around this image created by 613 employees handling 62 loan accounts and 900 new insurance policies. We must have a bottom line board of directors, and the Minister had better appoint a bottom line board of directors. Perhaps there have been further additions as of this year, and I am not exactly sure what the paid-in capital of the corporation is at this point, but as of the end of December, 1982 the corporation had $651 million in subscribed capital and retained earnings. On the $651 million, it earned $1 million. This is perhaps less than one-tenth of 1 per cent; I am not very good at mathematics. However, the return was $1 million on $651 million. That is a pathetic return. That return represents an implicit subsidy to those persons and corporations who received export concessionary financing. Bearing in mind the fact that during 1982 the Government of Canada was paying on the average 15 per

September 27, 1983
Export Development Act
cent for its money, the $651 million really cost us 15 per cent, or very close to $100 million. For the $100 million we received back $1 million. The subsidy then was very close to $99 million.
When we are paying out that kind of subsidy, and that is what we did, we had better make sure that Canada is getting value for the subsidies. A new, hard-nosed private board of directors had better be appointed to review the situation, because the matter will be coming back to the House of Commons next year. As soon as the corporation's next annual report is through, it is required that the report be referred back to the House's Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. That is one of the amendments that was put through on Friday. 1 am sure the committee will be asking those very questions, and I am now drawing the amendment to the attention of the Government and to the directors of the corporation.
There are a great number of things that we need to do concerning trade in Canada. We rely on foreign trade. We are a country that produces some basic commodities in huge amounts. They must be sold to the world. We are a country that has some of the most highly educated young people in the world, probably a higher percentage than anywhere else. Those young people are learning skills and trade in highly technical fields. Our exports of technological equipment can beat down doors of the world markets. We need an export corporation and we need financial assistance and the drive and the enthusiasm of people out there to encourage our producers to produce and to sell our goods. The challenge of the corporation is to move Canada ahead in trade.
Unfortunately, over the years we, as a country, have slipped in the percentage of world trade. At one time we had very close to 6 per cent of the world's trade. We are now down to well less than 4 per cent of the world's trade. We have gone down about 50 per cent from our former position, and that cannot continue. We in this nation rely on trading with others for our prosperity. The corporation is one of our front line tools for trade. It had better start acting efficiently, effectively and dramatically to encourage and build our trade, or we in this House of Commons will want to know why.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to ask the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), who has declared that he is strongly in favour of added incentives for exporters in Canada, if this debate being conducted by the Official Opposition is a filibuster. I would ask him how many speakers he has put up on behalf of that Party in an attempt to stop us from coming forward with the increased funding that is necessary to do the job on behalf of Canadian exporters.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the Hon. Member was not here on Friday but he can be excused. The issue in the debate was that of parliamentary accountability. It had nothing at all to do with trade.
He does not understand.

That is right. He does not understand that. He does not understand because at some point he has taken the attitude that the Government knows best and he believes anything the bureaucracy tells him.
If he could read financial statements he would know that there was no need for this Bill to be passed in a mad rush. If there was any urgency the Government would have introduced the Bill for debate much sooner than last week. Even last week, with the most optimistic trade possibilities, the Government had enough credit on hand to finance Canada's exports without any additional capital requirements, or borrowing limit requirements, without any additional money toward order in council awards or order in council insurance appointments.
If the Hon. Member cares to examine the financial statement, he would find that at ten times the subscribed capital and earned surplus in the corporation it could borrow roughly $7 billion. He would also find that the corporation only owes the marketplace $4.5 billion. Therefore he would know that the corporation had the right to borrow well over $2 billion without this Bill ever coming before Parliament.
The Hon. Member does not understand the Bill yet he stands here and asks questions. He asks how many speakers we have put up. While I do not have the exact number, there are about 153. He asks why they were speaking. It is so that Parliament and Members of Parliament could ensure that this corporation and the Government which that Hon. Member represents is accountable to Parliament and not the bureaucracy.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The Chair ought to remind Hon. Members that questions, comments and replies should be brief and to the point. Is the Hon. Member standing to be recognized for a further question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that they cannot oppose the substance of what we are attempting to do, which is to facilitate the efforts of the Export Development Corporation in doing its job in a much expanded way on behalf of the private sector in this country. But what have they done? They got on the high horse of parliamentary accountability.
If the Opposition intends to adopt this practice not only with a Bill through which we are attempting to help those people who can really make our economy move in the days ahead but with every Bill we introduce, 1 simply want the Canadian people to know that that is obstruction and not constructive criticism.
What is your question?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I have heard other Hon. Members ask what the question was. Standing Order 35(1) provides for questions or comments and replies thereto.

Mr. Speaker, the reply is clear. This Party will stand up for Canadians, talk in the House and put forward constructive amendments. We will make sure that the agencies of the Government and the Government itself are accountable
September 27, 1983

to Parliament. We will make every effort and speak as long and often as necessary to make sure that that occurs. For the Hon. Member to say that this is a Bill with respect to trade and that our debate concerns trade is not to understand what occurred here for the past two and a half weeks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted that the Opposition is supportive of our efforts to aid the private sector to do its job of increasing our share of world trade. I am glad that they have come to that admission lately, however reluctantly.
If the issue is credibility, 1 would invite the Hon. Member to review the speeches which have been made in the House by Hon. Members from this side, including myself, dealing with the ways in which the Export Development Corporation is accountable to the people of Canada through our institution of Parliament. Let me summarize some of the ways in which that corporation is accountable. It is accountable to the Auditor General, the Comptroller General, the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates when additional borrowings must be approved, and to the Minister who is answerable in the House. He is an excellent Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) who has been making great efforts on behalf of Canadian exporters to make their goods known and better recognized in the marketplace of the world. It is through that approach that we have accountability.
The Opposition may not want that exact approach and prefer to have an opportunity to approve every single additional issue when the Export Development Corporation has to go to the marketplace. Surely that is an unreasonable constraint to impose on any operation which has to be flexible in meeting the needs of Canada's exporters. The House does not sit all year long and it must also deal with many other issues that come before us. Imagine what would happen if every new issue that the EDC wanted to bring out had to be brought before the House.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Member has gone on for an additional two minutes. I think he has made his point.

Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the Hon. Member did not read the Bill. He will find that under the existing Act, and as it was amended on Friday, borrowing by the Export Development Corporation can take place without the corporation ever coming to the House and without ever having the approval of any committee of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Opposition Whip; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Or without the Minister's approval.

Indeed, without the Minister. Though it may have some problems with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). He will know that the controls which we wanted were ones which the Minister finally gave us. They demanded that there be some equity capital relationship between borrowing and debt. We would then have some element of control over what the corporation in fact borrows so that it cannot get itself into some of the problem situations such as companies like Canadair and de Havilland were allowed to get into by the
Export Development Act
Government. We have been very responsible by forcing the corporation to have a relationship in borrowing ten times the paid-in capital and retained earnings of the corporation. That kind of change, which the Government finally accepted on Friday after resisting it for seven days of debate, makes quite a difference in the control that Parliament and the people have over this corporation and its actions.

Mr. Speaker, I want to be fairly brief this morning but I wish to continue the comments made by the Parliamentary Secretary about the amendments that passed through the House on Friday. 1 also wish to talk about the Bill itself in general.
[DOT] (M50)
There were two significant points about the amendments which were passed on Friday with all-Party support. The first was that there will now be more accountability to Parliament and its committees by the Export Development Corporation. I think that is a very good and positive step. It is the kind of step which should be taken with other Crown corporations in this national Parliament.
The Province of Saskatchewan, under the premiership of Tommy Douglas back in the 1940s, established a special Crown corporations committee of the legislature on which sat Members of all Parties. The annual reports of the provincial Crown corporations are referred automatically to that committee each and every year. Also, every year the officers of the Crown corporations must go before the committee, talk about their plans and justify what they have done in the year gone by. That is a very good step. It is the kind of thing we should have in this Parliament where automatically the reports of Crown corporations are referred to the relevant committee for cross-examination and discussion by Parliamentarians. I think that is very important.
I am a very strong supporter of Crown corporations. I suppose that is true of all Parties, including the Conservative Party. I can look at Peter Lougheed in Alberta with PWA and his investments in the oil industry, or Bill Davis in Ontario with the purchase of part of Suncor and other Crown corporations. I can look at the federal Crown corporations and the ones we have established in the three Provinces which we have governed in the last number of years. It is very important that they be more accountable and more responsive to the wishes of Canadians. That is the message we tried to get across in this debate, and we have succeeded to a certain degree by the amendments that were accepted last Friday.
The second important point about the amendments is that Parliament finally has a little say over what a Bill should contain or what the EDC should look like, rather than the Cabinet or the executive exercising an almost autocratic say in a situation where we have a majority Parliament. I think that is a good step as well. Where we have a majority Parliament in our system, all too often because of the hang-up on the confidence vote, the lack of free votes or things of that sort and the lack of clout of committees, the executive, the Prime Minister's office or the Minister's office, has much too much

September 27, 1983
Export Development Act
power and Parliament itself has much too little power. Those were the two very significant points about the amendments which all three Parties supported last Friday to Bill C-110 respecting the Export Development Corporation.
Another point I want to make is that this is only a beginning. We have to move more and more toward a system of economic democracy where ordinary citizens, workers, farmers, consumers, producers and business people have more say over the economic direction of the country. For years we have talked about and exercised political democracy and voted every two to five years. The time has come in the twentieth century to start talking about the ways and means of achieving real economic democracy so that the ordinary citizen, regardless of one's income, has more influence upon the direction of society. I believe we can do that as well in the Crown corporations of this land.
World trade is very important for Canada. In fact, it is more important in our country than in most other countries of the world.
[ Translation]
International trade has always been very important to Canada, because we do not have a large population, compared with the United States, France, Japan and other countries. In Canada, international trade represents about 25 per cent of our gross national product. In the United States, it is 12 or 13 per cent of GNP, the same in France and Germany, and perhaps less than 10 per cent in Japan. Export development is very important for creating jobs for Canadians, more 80 for us than for other countries, with the exception, for instance, of New Zealand, Australia and other countries with a small population. Mr. Speaker, the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) said earlier that our share of international trade has shrunk considerably in the last twenty years. For instance, between 1972 and 1979, it dropped from 4.9 per cent to 3.4 per cent. In only seven years we had this substantial drop in our share of world trade, notwithstanding the Export Development Corporation, the Government of Canada and all the speeches made by the Prime Minister and other Ministers during that time. Another interesting figure shows that between 1969 and 1979, the market share of Canadian exports dropped 33 per cent. That is a lot.

With those kinds of statistics it is easy to see that, despite the fact trade is so important, our share of world trade is falling. This is one reason more and more people in the country are unemployed each and every year.
World trade is becoming more and more aggressive. We can look at the French, Germans, Japanese, Americans, British and even the Third World. Despite the fact that we in Canada have increased our exports dramatically, in the last ten years or 15 years our share of world trade has fallen.
I would like to indicate one more specific which I think puts into perspective the need for being more aggressive and ensuring that we are more competitive with the French, Germans
and Japanese. Between 1969 and 1979 we increased our trade at an annual rate by some 15.1 per cent. We may say that that is a tremendous increase or growth in our trade, but developing countries increased their trade at an annual rate of 23.1 per cent, or 8 per cent faster than Canada. My feeling is that we will go more and more slowly in terms of our increase in trade in comparison with the rest of the world.
I want to spend a minute or two on other matters which are very relevant to the Export Development Corporation and to trade in general. I do this because of the tremendously high unemployment rate in the country. I refer to our failure as a nation in expanding our manufacturing base. I see the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) in the House. He has often mentioned our failure as a country to develop, protect, expand, modernize and make competitive our manau-facturing base with the Europeans, Japanese and Americans.
Back in 1970 our deficit in manufactured goods was $2.5 billion. In 1981 our deficit in finished goods had risen from $2.5 billion to $21 billion-a tremendous deficit in finished products. In finished products we have many skilled jobs with which to put people to work. The EDC must do a much better job in terms of financing, insuring and promoting in every way it can under the Act the export of Canadian manufactured goods around the globe. Perhaps it is one of the sad commentaries in our country that since its inception, or even earlier, we have been an exporter of raw materials and an importer of finished goods. If we go back to Samuel de Champlain in 1608, the French exported beaver pelts from Canada and purchased finished goods in return. We are no longer exporting great quantities of beaver pelts, but we are still following the same philosophy of exporting raw material and importing finished goods. The EDC has to do something to try to change that trend.
The other point that disturbs me about the Export Development Corporation and our trade in general is that too much of the export financing done by the EDC, and I think the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) will agree with this, is going to a few large companies and much too little is going to small business.
I believe that the large multinational corporations are powerful. They can look after themselves. They have a lot of funds, resources and contacts around the world. The EDC does not have to worry about financing many of these big corporations in different parts of the world. Instead, it should be concerned about helping the small business people across this country.
A couple of years ago a special committee of this House studied the possibility of establishing a national trading corporation. In its report, it stated that 37 per cent of businesses in Canada did not know the Export Development Corporation even existed and only 29 per cent of businesses in this country ever used the EDC. It shows there is something missing when only 29 per cent use EDC and only 62 per cent know it exists. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) may want to comment on this later.
September 27, 1983

In its statement of May 24 last, the Economic Council of Canada said to us that between 1969 and 1980 only 16 companies had availed themselves of over 50 per cent of the loans from the Export Development Corporation. One company had a loan on 40 different occasions between 1969 and 1980. Some 138 companies used EDC loan financing between 1969 and 1980. There were 415 loans, and 16 companies accounted for well over half of the loans from the Export Development Corporation. That is another point that is very important. If the EDC is to be seen to be working and efficient, it should put more emphasis on aiding and assisting small business in this country, which employs 60 per cent or more of the Canadian population.
Those are some of the important matters that we should look at. There are a number of other points on trade and the EDC that 1 have mentioned at other times. One is that we must ensure that our trade policy jibes with our foreign policy, that we not just try to make a buck for the sake of a buck, but that there be some moral purpose to the kind of trade we are trying to develop. As I mentioned, we should try to push more manufactured goods.
I have often tried to point out to the House that before we can have a proper trade policy, we need a proper economic and industrial policy so that we know where we are going. We need a more planned economy. We should specialize in a few areas that are natural to our country. We should modernize our industry so that we can preserve some jobs and create others. These are some points the EDC should be working on as well.
In conclusion, 1 am pleased that last Friday afternoon we reached an all-Party agreement to make the Export Development Corporation more accountable to this House. A number of people worked on this for quite some time. I hope the Government will look on this as a precedent and automatically refer the annual reports of all Crown corporations to the relevant committees from here on in. This is very important because of the number of Crown corporations that we have. Most of us in this House support Crown corporations. We must ensure that they are accountable and are in step with the policies and wishes of the Parliament of Canada.
The last point I want to make is that this Parliament should have more say over Government policy when we have a majority Parliament. All too often it is the executive or the Prime Minister who run the show and want to use us as a rubber stamp. In a healthy democracy in the twentieth century we need to have more legislative input and clout from the ordinary Member of Parliament. It is time we had some radical parliamentary reform so that we can move in that direction. I do not see why the Prime Minister should have the right in our system to appoint heads of Crown corporations and to appoint unilaterally heads of regulatory agencies and national boards. If we are to have a truly democratic parliamentary system, the Prime Minister should only nominate. That nomination should go before the relevant committee of this House. The committee would cross-examine the nominee and either ratify or reject the nomination of the Prime Minister. That would be true parliamentary democracy. 1 hope that
Export Development Act
is the direction this Parliament will go in the years that lie ahead.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first want to indicate to the Members why the Minister responsible, the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan), is not here today. The Minister is attending the quadralateral meetings at Meach Lake which Canada is hosting on questions of international trade. He has asked me expressly to thank the Members of the House for the co-operation they have given, especially on Friday when we were able to reach a rather monumental agreement and come to a House Order to pass this through third reading today.
I would like especially, with the Minister's admonition to me, to thank the Hon. Members for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), Calgary South (Mr. Thomson), Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and the Members on this side of the House who have been instrumental in bringing concerns to the attention of the Minister which ultimately resulted in the amendments that were made at report stage on Friday and which are now part of the Bill that will receive third reading today.
In my role almost as a mediator between sides, I found it a very exciting prospect to find ways to accommodate the valid expressions of concern of the Opposition and the very valid need for moving forward with necessary legislation on the part of the Government. 1 can assure Members on both sides of the House that I intend to play that role as actively as I possibly can in the future to see whether we can make Parliament work the way all of us want it to make it work-much more effectively, moving forward with legislation on which all of us can agree.
There is no doubt that the legislation was necessary. The Export Development Corporation has a very vital function in our economy. The way our economy is structured, certainly international trade cannot be anything but seen by this House as being of the utmost importance, and the Export Development Corporation facilitates that greatly. I was interested in some of the comments made by the Members for Mississauga South and Yorkton-Melville. I am sure some of those comments will be reiterated by other Members as the debate continues.
Through the amendment process we have emphasized the notion of accountability of Crown corporations to Parliament, although I would say that accountability to Parliament on a less frequent basis was certainly part of the legislation as it was brought before us. Parliamentary accountability through the reference of the annual report, should we continue with the provisional rules now before the House, would have been the case in any event. The amendment brought forward by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South ensures that should the provisional House rule not continue beyond the deadline that we have set for ourselves in the trial period, automatically that annual report will be referred to committee, should there be

September 27, 1983
Export Development Act
changes to the Standing Orders away from what we now have. It was always our intention that these changes to the Standing Orders would continue and, therefore, the annual report of the Export Development Corporation would have automatically been referred to a committee for scrutiny. We have a different form of parliamentary accountability perhaps from the point of view of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South and others, and that accountability has been strengthened. Certainly I was always of the opinion that the Export Development Corporation would have to be accountable to Parliament in a very meaningful way even as the Bill was originally introduced.
1 was interested to hear the comments made by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South with regard to the Economic Council report. That was a report we in committee looked at with great care, indeed, representatives of the Economic Council came before the committee to make representations about the Export Development Corporation and to present their report on export financing. I too share the concerns of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South and others with regard to the role of the Export Development Corporation vis-a-vis the role of other private sector intermediaries in financing foreign trade.
During those committee hearings we heard a great deal with regard to how other countries come to joint arrangements between private sector financial intermediaries and state controlled export financing arms. 1 would hope that in the future we in Canada would indeed see some movement toward more joint ventures and more loan guarantees made by the Export Development Corporation to ensure not only the widest possible range of export financing mechanisms available but that the market penetration of sound export financing can be as deep as possible without having to depend solely on one agency.
My hon. friend referred to the 613 employees of the Export Development Corporation. Contrary to his views, when one is talking about penetrating a massive market with tens of billions of dollars worth of export, 613 is really quite a small number of employees to do the kind of job that we would like to see done in the export financing field. I would hope that those 613 employees could be used more intensively through the use of joint ventures with private sector financial intermediaries.
Expanded coverage and the presence of export development financing through the Export Development Corporation to a wider range of firms are ideas that we in the Finance Committee were very concerned about and we probed quite deeply into those matters. 1 would certainly be of the view that the facilities of the Export Development Corporation should first be made known and then made available to a much wider range of firms, and I refer both to the nature of export business as well as to the size of firms.
Obviously, given the size of the Export Development Corporation, export financing through the corporation will be more favourably disposed toward export financing for very large
deals through very large firms. I believe it was the original intention of the Export Development Corporation to finance the very large deals that the private sector would be reluctant to finance. 1 can certainly see a role, however, for the Export Development Corporation, through loan guarantees and other kinds of joint arrangements, in making its facilities available to the smaller firms that have a very important role to play in the export future of the country.
With regard to the area of co-operation, I might, Mr. Speaker, just as an aside, say a few things about the structure of our private financial intermediation system. At the moment, as you know, Mr. Speaker, there are certain restrictions on our financial institutions with regard to the nature of business that they can undertake in the marketplace. The chartered banks, the Canadian owned and operated banks, the Schedule A banks, have restrictions on the kinds of things that they can do. Subsidiaries of foreign-owned and controlled banks, our Schedule B banks, have very serious restrictions on the kinds of business that they can undertake. That matter is currently before the Finance Committee and we are about to make recommendations with regard to how we should look at the question of Schedule B banks, what the nature of their presence should be and whether or not some of the restrictions, in particular the 8 per cent ceiling, should be changed or not.
Certainly these institutions, the chartered banks, the Schedule A and B banks, the trust companies, credit unions, co-ops, caisses populaires and insurance companies have in the past been separated into specific sectors of financial intermediation. My own personal view is that as a result of this we have precluded a great many innovative and creative arrangements that are now being undertaken in other countries to facilitate the financing of domestic and export operations that we could enjoy here in Canada.
1 would hope to see the Export Development Corporation form part of the renewed, reinvigorated and renovated system of financial intermediation that I see evolving in the minds of many parliamentarians here. This new system of financial intermediation could create the framework that would facilitate the kinds of changes that we have all been talking about with regard to trust company legislation and the kinds of changes that have been asked for with regard to life insurance and general insurance legislation as well as legislation with regard to caisses populaires, credit unions and other forms of financial intermediaries.
A more flexible and broader based set of financial institutions in the country could certainly compete in many different markets outside of those which are currently available to them. The Export Development Corporation then could play a very major catalytic role by ensuring that export financing was made widely available in the country, not only to large firms but to small firms and to a wider array of economic and commercial activities.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to the comment made by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville who said that he was a great advocate of a planned economy. The only thing that I could say about that is that "planned"
September 27, 1983

has a tendency to become obsolete, which is why we have the phrase "planned obsolescence".
1 am very much opposed to the notion that the state somehow has the kind of insight and intuition that would make it possible for it to plan the future from the centre. 1 do not think we can do so, and certainly the view of the Government is that we should not even try to do so.
The essence of what I have been saying, Mr. Speaker, is that we need to try to make our economic system, and especially in this case our system of financial intermediation and arrangement of financing, more flexible, more adaptable and more driven by the real needs and demands for services in the marketplace. It certainly is not my view that we can somehow plan and direct where financing should take place and what kinds of businesses certain financial intermediaries should engage in. Perhaps in the 1940s and 1950s when things were so much simpler, it was possible for governments to say: "This is an area of business that you as a financial intermediary can get into and this is an area that another financial intermediary can get into but you cannot compete with one another."
If our intermediaries are going to be able to compete in today's world, if they are to be first-rate and provide the best and cheapest services to Canadians for the purposes we all want to see, then we will have to have financial intermediaries that are capable of adapting and changing and working together by coming to joint arrangements and finding ways of providing those financial services at the cheapest possible cost in the most efficient ways. That means more flexibility, more adaptability and that we need to have a bottom-up type of financial system as opposed to a top-down, centrally planned financial system. I think that that kind of a view toward financial intermediation and financial institutions in the country is precisely the same kind of view that we will have to take toward an industrial policy, because an industrial policy that is top-down directed will be just as inflexible and prove over time to be just as obsolete and ineffective as would a financial system that is top-down directed. It has to be bottom-up, market-oriented and responsive to changing needs.
If anything is certain in the future of this country, it is that change will occur as fast as it has in the past, not slower. There is no time for bureaucratic adjustment to change; it has to be bottom-up. What the Government has to do is to ensure that it can remove the barriers and restrictions that may hold up the development and growth of the economy and our financial institutions. They must provide the kind of flexibility that will facilitate change so that we can create the jobs and wealth that the country needs in the future.
The Export Development Corporation has a vital role to play because it is oriented toward megaproject financing. As many Hon. Members have said, it needs to take into consideration how it can work as a catalyst with private financial institutions in the future to get financing from them as opposed to depending on parliamentary approval for major infusions of new capital. We are talking about a maximum of
Export Development Act
$15 billion in lending from the Export Development Corporation. I cannot see a situation where Parliament would be willing to expand that base greatly. We must find ways to get the maximum leverage out of that $15 billion and the other facilities available to the Export Development Corporation in order to improve ways that our Schedule B banks, our Schedule A banks and other financial institutions can expand export financing and Canada's presence in export markets.
Hon. Members opposite have put forward very good ideas on this subject. The Export Development Corporation should not see itself as a "stand alone" agency doing most of its financing out of its own coffers; it should be a catalytic agent to ensure that financing for megaprojects is done but also that, through loan guarantees and other mechanisms, smaller firms have access to export financing.
1 should like to thank Hon. Members for their co-operation. The Minister is grateful for the co-operation that has resulted in the House order that will see the legislation pass third reading this afternoon. In my role with the Government House Leader, I look forward to seeing that kind of co-operation in the future to ensure that we move the nation's business ahead as the people expect.
Mr. Speaker, 1 wonder if the Parliamentary Secretary could advise us whether the international trade meeting is dealing with concessional financing, which is implicit in this Bill?

This Party believes in co-operative planning. We believe in planning with regions, with different sectors of the economy, but we certainly believe that the federal Government has the responsibility to take leadership in economic matters.

Mr. Speaker, in the remarks of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), directed to the Hon. Perhaps there is something lacking in my education, but I would have assumed that anyone would consider that planned obsolescence, as much as anything could be, is an invention of the marketplace, whether one talks about light bulbs, automobiles or vacuum cleaners which are geared to break down in a matter of two or three years in order to keep the market going. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What I meant by the comment "planned obsolescence" was that any central planning structure tends to create for itself the conditions for its own obsolescence. The problem with central planning bureaucracies, whether they be corporate, government or institutional of any kind, is that they do not change. As change occurs inevitably in our society and in our world they, by their very nature, become obsolete. Their planning function becomes obstructionist as opposed to creating and promoting the kind of change which the future demands. What I am saying, therefore, Mr. Speaker, is that all the good intentions which are behind the establishment of major planning functions lead directly to the establishment of a bureaucracy which, instead of planning for the future, starts to deal with planning to maintain its own existence, which in fact is counter to the notion of change in the future. That is the kind of thing I was talking about. Central planning leads to its own destruction by its very nature.

However, it may be necessary because as long as we have the current situation where directors are simply a cosmetic appointment by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), we really have no way of effectively causing the chief executive officer to be accountable to the board. And that is at the heart of the control of a Crown corporation. If you have a chief executive officer who is appointed, as presently, by the Prime Minister, to whom does he account? The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville, my hon. friend from Mississauga South and the Parliamentary Secretary have already referred to the fact that we have reached a milestone because we have finally agreed on a few insignificant amendments. I would like to compare that to rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic. That is about the size of it. The Liberal Government has moved only one millimetre in those terms.
The Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) was asking whether we were Filibustering this Bill. He is darned right, we did filibuster the Bill for a very good reason. The

Hon. Member for Willowdale completely missed the point of the debate. If he does not understand that the people of Canada care about the Canadian Dairy Commission and the $1.4 billion which Canadair has thrown down the drain, about the waste and extravagance and the uncontrolled operations of the Crown corporations of Canada, then he has missed the entire point of the debate. He has the nerve to stand up in this House and ask if we were filibustering. Let him read Friday's Hansard and then he will learn what happened.

We are trying to represent our constituents. Apparently the Hon. Member for Willowdale does not seem to be concerned. Does he think that his constituents are not concerned about the $200,000 worth of extravagance indulged in by the head of the Canadian Dairy Commission? How does he feel about that? What we are debating in this House, and what we were debating in this House, are the principles involved in controlling Crown corporations. The EDC legislation happened to be a Bill on which the Members on this side of the House and the New Democratic Party could put forward their views about the lack of control over Crown corporations.
As you might gather, Mr. Speaker, my concerns with respect to Crown corporations are two-fold. First of all, all 282 of us in this institution have done a lot of work over the last 18 months on parliamentary reform. There is a willingness on all sides of the House to come to grips with this important issue because what is at stake is the credibility of this institution and every Member. The same is true as it relates to Crown corporations. If we do not come to grips with this issue, Mr. Speaker, every Member of this House suffers and the institution itself will suffer. Look at the things happening in the Canada Dairy Commission. What do you think the Canadian people think of this man who heads the commission? Abuse of public trust, that is what it is. You know that, Members opposite know it, in fact every Member of this House knows it, and we all cringe a little bit.
Secondly, my concern is the proliferation of Crown corporations. One cannot keep up with them. I had from the Treasury Board a list showing 319 Crown corporations. It spelled out the subsidiaries and their classification. I said to my secretary that I would like to get that list updated or make sure it is up-to-date because the list was published last December. Do you know how many more we have today? Twelve new ones. They are just growing like weeds and no one on the other side wants to get their arms around the issue.
We in this House all know how important this issue is. Crown corporations represent 50 per cent of the Gross National Product, employ 263,000 people with $67 billion in assets.

Export Development Act
Federal Government appropriations on their behalf amounted to $6.5 billion last year. I cannot even comprehend $1 billion, let alone $6.5 billion.
I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, about the reckless abandon with which we are creating these Crown corporations. Every time we create one we deprive Canadians of a little bit more of their freedom, the freedom to innovate. We take away their motivation. If we are to be internationally competitive, Mr. Speaker, the solution to our problem lies with Crown corporations because their very thrust is not to be competitive. They are not bottom-line oriented. In a good many cases maybe they should not be. There is a good and valid reason for many Crown corporations. They have a legitimate role to play, they are a legitimate tool of Government where you want to give autonomy to a particular entity to accomplish a mission. But the unceasing proliferation of Crown corporations in Canada is sapping our willingness and ability to go out and compete in a very tough world today.
I have no quarrel with the Export Development Corporation, Mr. Speaker. As a matter of fact, on balance 1 think it does a pretty good job. 1 do question some of its practices but by and large it is fairly well managed. So the point is, and 1 want to stress this to the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson), that we are not condemning the functions or purposes of the EDC. There is no one on this side who has condemned those objectives and it would be wrong for anyone to conclude from Hon. Members' remarks that we were opposed to the EDC. But please understand that we are trying to focus public attention on this enormous and complex problem of Crown corporations which the Government opposite does not seem to want to come to grips with. Quite the contrary, it goes out and creates a monster like the Canada Development Investment Corporation. I think this is scary.
When I take the Parliamentary Secretary's remarks about centralized planning and the need to be market oriented and compare them with the formation of this monster-and I say "monster" knowingly-the CDIC, I can see that the primary function of that corporation is really to further state capitalism. The men who run it make no bones about it. Senator Austin, father of this legislation, makes no pretence about it. He says we are creating the CDIC to advance the cause of state ownership. It is part and parcel of the Canadian industrial policy of this Government. Oh, he said it, and so have Mr. Maurice Strong and Mr. Joel Bell.

The reason it is so difficult to come to grips with this issue is that we cannot sort out and put in a separate compartment the commercial or bottom-line functions of a Crown corporation and what 1 would call the public interest functions. So what we do is put them together and we ask the chief executive officer and board of directors to manage that corporation, and they have to weigh every single day in every decision they make whether or not the venture is going to be profitable and whether or not it is in the public interest.
This is at the heart of the problem of Crown corporations and their accountability. Unless we can find a means to segregate those functions within a corporation that should be bottom-line oriented, putting those into a separate compartment and then over here, on the other side, putting those public interest functions into another compartment, very clearly and succinctly spelling out the mandate to the chief executive officers and the board of directors, we will never come to grips with the accountability of Crown corporations, because-and it is only human nature-it is very easy to cloud the issue. If I make a mistake, if I pull a boner in a company and I can say that it does not show up in the bottom line, and one can say that I did not make a profit this year, it would not be because I really made a commercial mistake, but, rather, because I acted in the public interest. Probably no one but the employees or very close associates of the chief executive officer will know the difference. Certainly Parliament and the taxpayers of Canada will not know.
This is at the heart of the issue, together with the appointments of the board and of the chief executive officer, which are all so crucial, in my view, to controlling the operations of Crown corporations.
Let me just return to the subject of the Canadian Development Investment Corporation for a moment. This is the mandate of the Canadian Development Investment Corporation:
The objects of the Corporation are:
(a)	to assist in the creation or development of businesses, resources, properties and industries of Canada;
(b)	to expand, widen and develop opportunities for Canadians to participate in the economic development of Canada through the application of their skills and capital in any activities carried on by the Corporation;
(c)	to invest in the shares or securities of any corporation owning property or carrying on business related to the economic interests of Canada;
(d)	to invest in ventures or enterprises, including the acquisition of property, likely to benefit Canada; and
(e)	to carry out all activities in the best interests of Canada, operating in a commercial manner.
That is a very clear set of objectives. That means that the corporation can do absolutely anything under the sun. To whom does it report? It reports to the Prime Minister essentially. That is what it is all about, with no due regard, going through the motions. It sends us some financial statements. It really just reports on money spent. However, there is no clear-cut, succinct mandate by which we can hold the CDIC, its officers and the board of directors accountable, and that is the point. It can muddy the water and confuse all of the

decisions that it makes because it has cats and dogs and rats. One just cannot sort it out.
I am not trying to suggest that Parliament should attempt to be a manager. That is not the role we are here to play. I want to emphasize this point. In terms of accountability, I am not suggesting for one minute that Parliamentarians become managers of Crown corporations. Etowever, 1 am suggesting that we as Parliamentarians must come to grips with this issue of accountability if we are to save our own credibility. It is a vital issue. There seems to be an unwillingness to come to grips with it.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE MEASURES TO LIMIT IMPORTATION OF FOREIGN-BUILT SHIPS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, according to a press release from the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association, more foreign-built ships and floating equipment were registered in Canada in the first eight months of 1983 than in the entire year of 1982. If all the figures provided by Mr. Walsh, president of the Association, are accurate, it is clear that the Canadian Government should immediately take the necessary corrective action. The situation in our shipyards is indeed alarming. I am thinking, for instance, of the Davie shipyards in Lauzon, whose performance in terms of jobs has in recent years been in the 1,500 to 2,500 range. The figures for August, however, indicate that employment has dropped to 960 workers, and although construction on the CN Marine ferry will provide employment for the coming months, the future does not seem very promising for this shipyard which is the principal employer in the Quebec City area. Last January, the Government promised to get legislation through the House that would provide better safeguards for shipyard workers by restricting imports of foreign-built ships and providing guarantees with attractive provisions.
1 therefore urge the Government to have these measures adopted immediately, with the consent of the Opposition parties, which for once will have a chance to let their actions speak louder than their words.

subsubtopic: INCREASED INITIAL PAYMENT FOR BARLEY URGED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, about three weeks ago the Canadian Wheat Board suggested an increase in the initial payment for barley. As well, Cargill and the United Grain Growers have asked the Treasury Board to approve an increase in the initial payment to $110 per metric tonne, yet elevator operators and Canadian barley growers are still waiting for a decision.
While No. 1 feed barley has been trading in recent weeks at $160 per tonne or more on the export market out of Thunder Bay, the Wheat Board is paying farmers a mere $95 per tonne. Is it any wonder that farmers are reluctant to haul their barley to elevators? As a result, the Wheat Board is in danger of not having enough barley to meet its exports demands.
This ridiculously low initial price is causing another problem. Because the Wheat Board buys the majority of the Canadian barley crop, it virtually controls even the non-Board domestic price. Therefore, non-Board barley has sold domestically at just under $130 per tonne in recent weeks.
The discrepancy between the world price and the Wheat Board's initial payment for barley is far too great. Barley growers should not have to wait a full year until a final payment reimburses them for the difference.
It is critical that the Cabinet immediately approve an increase in the initial payment for barley. Its failure to do so to date illustrates the Government's inability to understand the financial needs of Canada's cash-starved farmers.

subsubtopic: REQUIREMENT THAT SENIOR CITIZENS MAKE QUARTERLY PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Government legislation requires that income tax, if it is not deducted at source, be paid in quarterly installments by taxpayers. Unfortunately this requirement causes undue suffering and hardship to many senior citizens.
Many of those who are retired live on the proceeds of a modest pension and they supplement this pension income with the interest earned from investments and savings. Canada Savings Bonds, because of their security, have been a prime source of investment for many pensioners. Certainly the nation has benefited as a result of the support many have given to Canada Savings Bonds. However, the interest on Canada Savings Bonds is paid once a year, in November, yet people are required to pay in income tax in quarterly payments, three of which fall due prior to November. In effect the Government wants its money back before it has paid it out.
For senior citizens who depend on Canada Savings Bond interest as an important part of their income, quarterly installment payments are a real hardship. Some are forced to borrow at commercial rates to make these installment payments.
I would like to draw to the attention of the Minister of Revenue the hardship that this regulation has caused, and 1 urge that the legislation be amended to permit payment of income tax on Canada Savings Bond interest after the interest is received in November.

Consumer and Corporate Affairs licensed contractors are not paying their subcontractors for removing urea formaldehyde foam insulation from Manitoba homes. Therefore the subcontractors have placed liens against 150 properties in Manitoba and work has remained unfinished. Will the Minister inform the House what she will do to correct this situation, and particularly what action she is planning to take to assist those home owners in Manitoba who will face the winter with no outside walls for protection against the cold weather?

The President of the Canadian Saltfish Corporation told the Macdonald Royal Commission that the number of fishermen in Newfoundland and Labrador must be reduced from the present total of 26,000 to some 12,000 if the fishery is to become viable. This amounts to a reduction of some 14,000 jobs. I would like to ask the Minister if the President, when making that statement, was reflecting government policy. If so, what alternative employment opportunities has the Minister to offer these 14,000 people?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am happy to report to the Hon. Member that the policy of the Canadian Government was made public by myself some months ago. subtopic: THE LATE OSIE F. VILLENEUVE TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: THE LATE OSIE F. VILLENEUVE TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yet another of our colleagues has passed away. I refer to Osie Villeneuve, who was a very strong Parliamentarian, a dedicated servant of his people in his constituency at both the federal and provincial levels.
Although his time in Parliament was short by comparison with his tenure in the provincial legislature, he was here in the years of the Government headed by the late Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker and was very highly regarded by Mr. Diefen-baker when he was Prime Minister.
Osie Villeneuve was a fitting representative of that area where the strains of Scottish Highlander and French-speaking Canadian so felicitously merged together to produce a society with a charm and flavour all its own. He was in every sense a "man from Glengarry" and a strong proponent of the Scottish as well as his native culture. He represented a county where Scottish and French Canadian lumbermen erected a tradition and history of sturdy self-reliance and dependence on their own efforts for survival. He was a familiar figure at the Games which are yearly held in Maxville, where his funeral is scheduled to take place on Thursday next.
Representing an area which was the early home of Ralph Connor, whose family name was, of course, Gordon, where there are still memories of John Sandfield MacDonald and where Simon Fraser lies buried, he knew well how to mingle the strains of both our ancient races. In this House in the late fifties and early sixties, Osie Villeneuve was a repository of down-to-earth common sense with a strong feeling of affection for his people and his Province.
His passing represents the second death of a former Member in a few days and our sympathies go to his family, his widow Alma, and his sons Brian, Bernard and Ronald; and also to his riding and to Premier William Davis, under whose banner he served and was serving at his death.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: THE LATE OSIE F. VILLENEUVE TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
The Late Osie F. Villeneuve
Madam Speaker, I would like to rise on behalf of the Government of Canada to pay tribute to a provincial colleague from my constituency and that of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Ethier). Osie Villeneuve, as the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has indicated, served this House for six years. He also served the provincial legislature for 29 years, a total of 35 years of very dedicated and devoted service to the people of eastern Ontario. Mr. Villeneuve's many years of public service at the federal and provincial levels is indicative of the concern and interest he demonstrated on countless occasions towards the well-being of his area and its citizens.
My experience with Mr. Villeneuve goes back much longer than the time I have been a federal Member of Parliament. It began during my days in business in the constituency which he served. One of the things I have always admired about Mr. Villeneuve is that he always spoke out for what he believed in. Obviously every Member of this House has great respect for those like Mr. Villeneuve who dedicate their lives to serving the public in this manner.
During election times he was a fierce competitor, but to me what was most important was that between elections he was dedicated to the people of his area, regardless of one's political persuasion.
Those of us in eastern Ontario who had the privilege of knowing and befriending Osie will be comforted by the fond memories of his efforts on our behalf. He touched the lives of nearly every person in his constituency during his 35 years of service. He had a strong commitment to his family, his country, his constituency, and he will be sorely missed. To his wife Alma and his three sons, as well as to all members of the Villeneuve family, I would like to extend the Government's and my personal deepest sympathy during this time of remembrance.

subtopic: THE LATE OSIE F. VILLENEUVE TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I knew Osie Villeneuve well. I served with him in the Ontario legislature for 12 or more years and I remember him vividly. As was said earlier, he was a person who had a remarkable capacity for finding a compromise, and though he was a strong partisan he was able to put aside partisan differences on those occasions when finding solutions to difficult situations required that to be done. He was able, as is evidenced by the number of years he was successfully re-elected, to reach out and touch the constituents in his riding association and in his riding.
He seemed to have the capacity, Madam Speaker, as I recall from working with him, for finding in everything that was being done something that was worth while. People who came to the Ontario legislature to meet with Osie Villeneuve never went away with the impression that he somehow or other did not understand their problem or would not take some action to try to ameliorate it.
Therefore I want to join with my two colleagues in the House to say on behalf of my colleagues how sad we feel at his passing and I hope his family will at least feel the comfort that they surely must in knowing that he is well respected, well regarded and has provided a tremendous amount of service on behalf of so many people.

September 27, 1983

subtopic: THE LATE OSIE F. VILLENEUVE TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER

Madam Speaker, I had expected to rise before Question Period under Standing Order 21 to pay tribute to my colleague and friend, the Hon. Osie F. Villeneuve, MPP for Stormont-Dundas-Glengarry, but as you know, following discussions I had with you, Madam Speaker, I understand and accept your recommendation that honouring or paying tribute to distinguished personalities cannot and must not be done under Standing Order 21. Therefore I am pleased to join those who have spoken before me and add that we were all deeply saddened to learn of the death of the Hon. Osie F. Villeneuve from Maxville, Ontario.
Mr. Villeneuve represented the riding I presently represent from 1957 to 1962, and with the exception of that brief period he represented the population of Glengarry in the Ontario legislature at Queen's Park from 1948 until now, a remarkable 35-year career. On numerous occasions I had the privilege of working very closely with Mr. Villeneuve. Osie, as he is so well known to all of us, served his constituency with honour and dignity. He was a hard-working and dedicated servant. His door was always open to his constituents. He will be long remembered for the non-partisan manner in which he carried out his numerous mandates as a representative of both provincial and federal Governments. Osie will be missed by all.
