The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pinard (for Mr. Regan) that Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker,, just prior to the lunch hour adjournment, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Peterson) asked me why we chose to debate Bill C-l 10 for seven days with some 140-odd speakers. I would happily reply to that question.
Bill C-l 10, as the Parliamentary Secretary may know, was introduced in the House in May of 1981, two years and some months ago. When it was introduced into the House by the then Minister of State for Trade, he came to me as spokesman for Trade of the Conservative Party and asked me if we could very quickly dispense with the Bill. It did not seem to involve a great deal. I reviewed the Bill and agreed with him that it was not earthshaking, but I sought three amendments to the Bill. First, I wanted greater representation from the private sector on the board of directors of the Export Development Corporation. Second, I wanted the financial disclosure shown in the financial statements of the Export Development Corporation. I wanted the corporation to disclose the contingent liability with respect to the commitments the corporation had made to finance certain contracts at one rate of interest, then going out on the open market and having to finance those commitments at a higher rate of interest. Third, I wanted the Government to bring forward appropriations that were necessary to fund the Export Development Corporation from time to time. 1 wanted them brought before Parliament. The then Minister of State for Trade said; "I do not see any problem with those amendments. They seem perfectly reasonable. I think I can arrange to have those approved by my Cabinet."
Here we are, two years later, debating the Bill. They were very reasonable amendments that I put forward. We put those amendments forward in committee for over two years. We did not receive one civilized response in a period of two years to those simple, straightforward amendments, not one sign of willingness to amend the Bill in those reasonable ways. I say to the Parliamentary Secretary that that is why we were here in the House for seven days. That is why we put forth 140 speakers.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any further questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, in joining in the final debate on the Export Development Corporation Bill, I felt it might be helpful if I could underline what has really transpired with respect to the Bill. First, I would like to emphasize that Canada does need an important acceleration in our trade activity as far as the rest of the world is concerned.
September 27, 1983

There are several ways that we can consider the matter. I had an earlier opportunity to speak at report stage on the Bill and pointed out that on a world, global basis, Canada at one time had about 5 per cent of the total trade of the world, and that has now deteriorated to about 3.6 per cent. But perhaps I should have continued further at that time and pointed out that with respect to the components of our share of world trade the picture is even bleaker. I refer, of course, to manufactured products. We find that we once had over 4 per cent of the world's total share, but that has now deteriorated, as far as manufactured goods are concerned, to something over 2 per cent. 1 suggest, and this point has certainly been made by many business associations, such as the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, that if we could just regain our fair share of world trade, especially in manufactured and in semi-manufactured products, we would really cut our unemployment by half. Surely, when we face the reality that, first, there has been a steady deterioration under the emperor with respect to our share of world trade, and that perhaps half of the unemployment today is due to the fact that we have lost that fair share of world trade, we can see how relevant the debate is with respect to export-import trade generally, but specifically with respect to Bill C-110, the Export Development Corporation Bill.
Having said that, it is natural to ask what will be done about it. My first suggestion would be to make it extremely easy for business generally in Canada, and especially for the smaller businessman, to get their fair share of trade in the world market. This brings us to the essential question of whether the Export Development Corporation is serving the Canadian public, the businessman-and the small businessman specifically-adequately in relation to allowing them to participate in world trade. Coupled with that question, I believe we must consider whether Parliament is being given the opportunity to scrutinize, perhaps to make suggestions, and above all to be satisfied with what the Export Development Corporation is doing. It must not only be adequate but fair and attempting to achieve the goal we seek, which is to regain what we have lost in world trade.
This is where I feel the debate on Bill C-110 has been so relevant. I know that the trained seals on the other side are often impatient when we delay a Bill because we feel there are certain provisions that must be changed. We sought various amendments to this particular Bill. While we would like to have won them all, we agreed to accept amendments in the spirit of compromise which perhaps went only part of the way. At least, they were an improvement. Of course, I am referring to amendments to these blank cheques which the Government enjoys having Parliament authorize. At least we were able to have that measure tempered. More importantly, we were able to have a specific clause included in the Bill which will require the annual report and financial statements to be referred to the relevant committee of the House every year.
Having said that, let me underline why I feel it is so important that we have that type of parliamentary scrutiny.
Export Development Act
During the debate at report stage of this Bill, I mentioned that most Canadians would not believe it if they were told that of the approximately $2.5 billion total financing commitments and dealings that the Export Development Corporation handled in 1982, $957 million went to one company; Bombadier. I invite those who are interested to go to the Library and read the annual report from Bombadier. They will find it almost unbelievable that in relation to the size of that company, the Export Development Corporation would have felt justified in awarding it the benefit of almost $1 billion worth of financing. In 1982, for example, the total sales of Bombadier were $448 million. In one year, financing was approved which will result in an eventual benefit to that company of almost $1 billion in sales.
When we are dealing with a situation which represents almost 40 per cent of the total 1982 activity of the Export Development Corporation, surely it is relevant that we in the House ask if that was a wise course of action. Surely we must ask if there has been proper scrutiny and when we would have an opportunity to review the details of what the EDC is doing with respect to that one benefactor of financing.
Let me go further. How many in the Canadian public realize that one country has been given what is called an unconfirmed line of credit of $2.5 billion? Of course, I refer to an arrangement that was made some time ago in favour of China. While that may be a very sensible move for the people of Canada to make, surely we in the House owe it to our constituents to almost insist that the Government must be able to satisfy the Members of the House that the deal which it has in mind is fair, will serve the Canadian public, and particularly the smaller businessman since that is where EDC lacks fairness, before it enters into those kinds of transactions.
Furthermore, we have seen these disclosures of mismanagement of various Crown corporations in Canada. I could take the balance of my time just reading the names of the companies that are involved, such as Consolidated Computer and Canadair. Suffice it to say that there are billions of taxpayers' money not only for this generation but for generations to come that will be lost because of the ineptitude of the Government in running so many of these Crown corporations.
Again we find that the EDC plays a hand. While Bombardier received almost 40 per cent of the total activity of the EDC in 1982, a nice little company owned by the Crown called de Havilland picked up $200 million. Surely we must ask ourselves, if the Government saw fit to give assistance amounting to $200 million to one concern, a Crown corporation, whether that was the most suitable way to spend that money compared to ensuring perhaps 100 or 1,000 smaller businesses picking up a piece of that type of financing benefit.
While pointing out the de Havilland example, I think it is interesting to see to which countries that financing has been awarded. For example, in 1982 there was a financing facility awarded to a country called the United Republic of Came-room. It was for $25,190 million. As well, we see that Colombia picked up a couple of financings; one for $1,466 million and another for $1,460 million, both giving a benefit to

The aircraft built by de Havilland-

Did you ever hear of the Buffalo?

Clearly, when the Minister of National Defence keeps interjecting, we are getting to the quick. He knows that this is stuff the Government would just as soon have under the carpet and not much comment about.
Is that as much as you know about de Havilland? You should visit its aircraft plant in Toronto.

Let me emphasize that I am only giving an example of where EDC financing has been routed.
I could go through this for other companies that are very closely connected with the Government. Here is one in favour of de Havilland for $3.8 million to Malaysia. When we were dealing with an aggregate of $200 million in financing for the benefit of the Havilland, was that the most sensible way in 1982 for the Government of Canada to facilitate an export, as opposed to ensuring that hundreds of smaller businessmen received some part of the benefit? The question is as simple as that. I have yet, either in committee or in the House, to hear a Government Member or backbencher attempt to justify some of this type of financing to which I am referring.
1 have cited various countries, but what about the United States? Why, if we wished to sell to the United States aircraft manufactured by de Havilland, would we have to give them concessional financing through the EDC? In 1982 I see before me four financings, all for the benefit of de Havilland: one for $6,144,000; another for $11,858,000; another for $6,267,000; and a final one for $6,513,000, all to customers in the United States to allow them to buy de Havilland aircraft with our financing. Is that competition?
There is always a danger in this field when a company like de Havilland finds it tough to sell its products that if will start, through the Government of Canada, selling a financing program which the buyer cannot refuse. That, in turn, tends to weaken the infrastructure in the country. The selfsame Government which is hinting that it would like to see more free trade, especially with the United States, apparently overlooks the fact that to the degree we weaken our own in-country industrial capability and competitiveness and at the same time welcome free trade, basically we are asking for a situation that might develop where we will be overwhelmed by the American producer, and the manufacturing capability in Canada will be lessened still more.
What I am discussing is something which is actively being considered and reviewed in many of the so-called think-tanks both in Canada and the United States. If there is a debate which will ensue in the House, either in this session or the next, I hope that at least in part it centres on the critical question of where Canada's role will be through the 1980s and into the 1990s in terms of world trade. It is time we accepted that the academic, philosophical attitude of our emperor,
September 27, 1983

which may have been in vogue in the 1960s, has absolutely no relevance in the 1980s. If we continue to follow his impractical, unrealistic approaches, coupled with the confrontation which he seems to love so much, it will mean a much less wealthy Canada than we have every right to expect. The fall in real incomes in the last two years, which has started to accelerate as Statistics Canada pointed out, is just the beginning of a continuing fall if we do not start looking outward at the world and saying that Canada once again will regain its fair share of world trade. To do that, we must start looking at some of the issues 1 have touched upon today.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in the debate on a matter which is extremely important to Canadians. There are a minimum of 1.3 million Canadians now out of work, particularly young people. Every day 1 am in my riding I hear from people of all ages who say that they have lost their jobs. 1 am thinking of a man who told me he recently lost his job after 25 years. I am thinking of young people who tell me they cannot find their first job. As everyone here knows, the unemployment situation in Canada is unacceptable to all Canadians, whatever their politics or location in the country.
My contribution this afternoon is primarily based on a quotation by Jean Monnet, the father of the European Community, who said:
If a freely elected government makes a simple plan clear, free people can immediately adjust to it. Businessmen could plan investments, working people could plan savings, shopkeepers plan inventories, and farmers plan their fields.
I wish those words were posted on the walls here so that every one of us could look at them every day of the week. I think Mr. Monnet has stated a truth about which each one of us should be told frequently.
Evidently it is true that $1 billion worth of new exports creates approximately 40,000 jobs. It is clear that every time you create another $1 billion in exports you create an additional 40,000 jobs. The most cutting indictment that anyone can make of the Government is that it has willfully and intentionally created unemployment over the last number of years in order to fight inflation. It may have done something about inflation, but 1.3 million or more Canadians and their families have paid the full price for a policy designed to fight inflation and create additional unemployment.
I realize it is easy to be critical. This Bill asks what we on this side propose to do about the situation. Last year Professor Thibaut de Saint Phalle wrote a book entitled "Trade, Inflation, and the Dollar". Everyone could gain from reading the book. I am speaking personally and not on behalf of the Official Opposition in saying that some of his suggestions are applicable to Canada, this Government, and to all Canadians. I say that in the context that Canada, while being one of the
Export Development Act
luckiest countries in the world, is desperately in need of re-invigoration, renewed enthusiasm and, if 1 may coin a term, re-invigorization.
What can this Government and the Government in waiting do to help Canada increase its exports? Some of his suggestions are as follows: First, we can show greater interest in strengthening the world's monetary system. Second, we can show greater interst in, and response to, trade barriers created by other nations. Third, we can enact a clear national export policy. I know those opposite will say that they just announced one a few days ago. A press conference is now being held across the street with the trade ministers of the OECD, the United States, Japan and Canada.
Again I refer back to the quote of Mr. Monnet. How can a businessman plan a plant expansion, a new plant or whatever, when, until six months ago, the third option-the option that we get away from dependence on the United States and increase our multilateral approach with other countries in order to avoid dependence on the United States, greater trade with the United States and greater economic integration with the United States-was somehow morally unacceptable to Canadians? It is true that the recent trade policy of the Government indicates a greater sectoral integration with the United States.
My point is that you cannot jump from a national energy policy that blantantly discriminates against our major trading partner and other measures, such as FIRA, which sends a signal to the United States that it is not welcome in Canada, that we want to reduce rather than increase our economic ties with that country, and then say as we did six weeks ago, "Presto, Eureka, we are now converts, we want greater recognition of the geography between the two countries and greater recognition of the need for sectoral free trade with the United States". It is this flipping and flopping, going backwards and forward, going upside down and inside out, which has worsened many of our economic problems.
The Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. Pepin) in Question Period today stated that our investment statistics are bad. That should qualify as the understatement of the week. You cannot create permanent jobs without increasing investment. Jobs in large measure are a function of investment. If someone chooses to put his saving into a savings account at the bank, not as many jobs will be created as if he had put an addition on his house, opened a small dairy business or something along that line. That is the way to create long-term jobs in Canada. When you do not have this fundamental confidence among investors, you do not have the employment opportunities that Canada needs. I guess I had better speak briefly to the Bill.

Export Development Act

It is clear to all Members that last week we achieved something. There was all-Party agreement to the amendments. As you have probably heard one or two times today, Mr. Speaker, the borrowing capacity of the corporation is limited to ten times its paid-in capital in earnings rather than its authorized capital. Second, the authorized capital asked for of $2 billion has been reduced to Si.5 billion. This reduces the possible borrowings from $20 billion to $15 billion. Also of importance is the fact that in future the company will have to present its annual report and financial statements to the House of Commons, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, for examination. Finally, the right of the Government to take up loans and guarantees not appropriate to the corporation's activities has been reduced from $20 billion to $13 billion. For this we have to thank the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and recognize the goodwill of the Government on these matters.
The EDC can do part of the job, but it cannot do all of the job. We believe that it should be more accountable to Parliament. We have succeeded in persuading the Government to go along with this. I think it is within the grounds of relevance if in a personal capacity I say something about the proposed restructuring of the Department of External Affairs with respect to trade. You, Mr. Speaker, will be aware of the fact that External Affairs is to be integrated from top to bottom with the former trade section of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I invite the Hon. Member to state the relationship of the Bill, the Export Development Act, to what he is now raising, which is the subject matter of another Bill presently before a committee of this House.

It is indeed, Mr. Speaker. Thank you for correcting me on that. I believe this is relevant. I have before me the fascinating study of the Economic Council of Canada entitled, "The Bottom Line". It deals in large measure with trade. Chapter 10 deals with future trade policy. It talks about low interest loans. It is hard to argued that the EDC is not making low interest loans. In discussing an amendment last week, I stated that it may be making a lot of low interest loans and may in fact be engaging in more aid than trade.
We on this side strongly favour aid. However, I wonder whether the EDC should properly be confusing its role of financing trade with a role which more properly belongs to Cl DA, that of encouraging aid. This study talks about productivity. The author states that the productivity problem persists and that productivity has not grown for eight years.
How will this Bill increase productivity in the vital export industries which are now in a period of recession, as is the rest of the economy? How will we increase, through the Export Development Corporation, our trade in, for example, the export of manufactured goods?
It has already been pointed out in this debate that Canada's percentage of the total exports of manufactured goods was 3.3 per cent in 1960. In fairness, it is 4.2 per cent today. At the same time, Japan, for example, has gone from 5.3 per cent of total exports of manufactured goods in 1960 to 14.8 per cent. Surely, Sir, it seems to me that if Japan has had a simply phenomenal increase in its total exports of manufactured goods and Canada has had an increase of slightly under one percentage point, we should be looking at the programs used in Japan as compared to those used here.
What, for example, does Japan do with its equivalent of the Export Development Corporation? Is it modelled after our Export Development Corporation? Is it different, and if so, how does it differ? Should we not have a Bill in front of us now which would take Canada in the direction that Japan has gone in terms of exports? One may say that there are other programs dealing with that. Yes, it is true that there are other programs dealing with exports, but do we have the right kinds of programs? Do we have the right kinds of mechanisms in place that will allow Canadian manufacturers and exporters to increase their percentage of total world exports?
It has been pointed out by numerous speakers that the Export Development Corporation is not perfect. 1 think it is clear that this Bill does not perfect it. A number of speakers have referred to Professor Andre Raynauld who said that the EDC is:
-rapidly becoming a bureaucratic monster, borrowing and lending money, making unsound loans to foreign countries, extending its empire, and involving Canada in transactions and negotiations that are both costly and inefficient.
Professor Raynauld has compared the EDC to equivalent organizations in other countries and does not come to favourable conclusions.
The point cannot be made often enough that we on this side want to increase exports. We want to support anything and everything which will increase exports from Canada, because only in that way will we get Canadians back to work. At least I am persuaded that it is only by increasing exports that we will accomplish that.
I believe that it is a mistake for the Government to pretend that this Bill, as amended, is a panacea. It is not. It will take many other things to improve our trade position significantly. More important in my view, Sir, is that it is going to take a change of thinking on the part of the Government to improve our trade position, or, hopefully, it will take a new government which recognizes that the private sector can create jobs in the export market and that permanent jobs will only be created when Canada resumes its role as a secure place in which to invest, to work and to do business.
Let me give an example which perhaps makes what I am trying to say seem more real. Recently I heard of the case of a person in a European country who was engaged in the business of exporting beef. Somebody asked that person whether he did business in Canada. I am informed that the man rolled his eyes and said: "No, of course not. I do not do business in Canada". Asked why, he said that years ago he had had a contract with a Canadian company and that Canadian company, which I
September 27, 1983

obviously will not name, had botched the contract to the point that this man will never do business in Canada again. Unfortunately in this case, the European business community is a small business community. Stories like this get around rather quickly in the European business community, and they hurt you, Mr. Speaker, they hurt me and they hurt our constituents. If Canada is known as a country where one does not do business by choice, that hurts all of us.
I think that all of us in our own way within our own communities and businesses have to change our way of thinking. We have to become pursuers of excellence. 1 remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the book that is number one on the non-fiction bestseller list at the moment is entitled "In Pursuit of Excellence". It basically deals with management techniques of successful American companies. The book that is number two on the non-fiction bestseller list is called "Megatrends". I have read one of those books and I am now reading the other one. I wish everyone would read those books. Everyone would see that Canada has more going for it than any other country in the world. As we have all heard many times, Canada has people, resources, geography, infrastructures, social programs and access to markets. In my view, we have absolutely everything that is necessary to be number one in the world; yet, for various reasons, we are not number one at the moment.
We all must say to ourselves that from now on, we are going to pursue excellence in whatever our business or occupation is. We are going to get into this market or that market with a sense of urgency. Our businessmen must have a sense of urgency. You and I, Mr. Speaker, for different reasons, must have a sense of urgency as well.
Canadians need to develop an alertness to opportunities. Somebody was complaining the other day that there does not seem to be this sense of urgency in our business community at the moment. This sense of urgency must be encouraged. Anything that this Government or a new government can do that will encourage Canadians to do business around the world must, in my view, be done.
I will refer to some examples. I refer again to the book written by Mr. de Saint Phalle, and it seems to me that there is not enough appreciation of the need for exports in Canada.
Hear, hear!

It seems to me that the substitution of investments abroad by Canadian firms for a policy of marketing from Canada is one that must be encouraged.
My time is almost up. I do not have to tell you, Sir, how many Canadian companies have chosen to simply move out rather than continue here. There must be improved research and development in Canada. There must be more adequate training programs for the executives who are marketing Canadian products around the world.
May 1 continue, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, since the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) is the first
Export Development Act
speaker in a long time from that side of the House who has made sense, I have no objections to his continuing.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent to allow the Hon. Member to continue his speech?
Agreed.
No.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There is not unanimous consent.
Questions, comments? Debate. The Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert).

Mr. Speaker, it seems to be rather coincidental that my work this week has taken me into the consideration of two Bills, one in committee and one in the House, dealing with international trade. Bill C-152, the Government reorganization Bill, has of course a great deal to do with, shall we say, the framework of the department for international trade in the now omnibus Department of External Relations. This particular Bill, Bill C-110, deals with the financing of a good deal of our international trade. During the extensive debate at report stage my colleague, the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) and others, adverted to the problems of international trade in Canada. They spoke of its decline in an absolute and relative sense and the necessity for an increase, if we are to regain employment and economic activity. Those are not very simple problems.
Earlier, a Member of the Government referred to the fact that some 140 Members spoke at report stage in order to achieve the particular objective of having the Bill amended. The Government showed unbelievable gall in the size of borrowing authority it sought, the overcapitalization, and so on, of the Export Development Corporation. This could easily be halved and the corporation could still carry on as well as before. Unfortunately, however, it would have had to be accountable to Parliament if it wanted to increase the ceilings for borrowings and insurance as well as capitalization. We know that the Government wants to get as much blanket authority as possible so that it will not need to come to Parliament and give an accounting.
I do not know whether, in agreeing to the amendments of last Friday, we accommodated the real objective of the Government, that is, a gain of about one-third. There are ways of getting what you want. A typical bureaucratic way of achieving success is to overdemand and then make a concession. After extensive debate, concessions are eagerly seized upon by all concerned and a settlement is made. That is all very well but, of course, it was what the Government wants. I dare say we could have carried on debate and denied passage of the Bill at report stage, but then the Government would have brought in closure.

September 27, 1983
Export Development Act
1 am not going to comment on the amendments that were made or the Bill as it stands. I am going to say something that no one else referred to in the earlier stages of debate or in committee, where documents are produced, however. There is a stony silence from the media as well, as far as the representations made by public bodies and corporate interests with expertise in the field are concerned. This matter should therefore be brought up in this forum where there is wider public observation. 1 am going to refer to two bodies that made strong representations that I think are in keeping with what should be the philosophy of the corporation.
The Export Development Corporation was set up years ago to assist private financing-to assist Canadian exporters who, at that time, were doing well in the international field. The economies of Germany and Japan and the modern economies of Taiwan, Singapore and Korea were not set up, nor did we have competition from Brazil and other parts of the world where Canadians, to their surprise, now face competition. The attitude of many manufacturers and members of the public was almost, "How dare they?" They were used to the fat years after World War II when we lived in a euphoria of so-called international power and trade. The truth of the matter is that some of these countries have far more modern machinery and a younger and better trained work force which has a work ethic.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), referred to productivity. At the present time I am engaged in a study of productivity in the public and private sectors of Canada. The short answer to productivity is for the working public and the managing public to recover the work ethic. That is one of the, perhaps, simplistic ways of saying that we have to do better, not only in the public and private sectors but at all levels of government. We have been living in the land of the lotus eaters for the past generation and now we must work at regaining some of our lost trade.
In 1982 the Economic Council of Canada produced a report called "Intervention and Efficiency". After a rather notorious visit to Europe some six or seven years ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), he went on television in this country, without having discussed the matter with his Ministers, and indicated that the Government would become much more interventionist. We have seen what five to seven years of more intervention has done for efficiency. What has been the result as far as the Canadian economy is concerned? The Economic Council of Canada identifies one of the Government agencies which has had direct intervention, because it has excluded pretty well everyone else, and that is the Export Development Corporation. Canadians face greater risks in international trade than in domestic trade, and the financial requirements for it are greater. I will read those recommendations very quickly. The first one deals with the Export Development Corporation, and I quote:
We recommend that the Export Development Corporation gradually move towards providing export credit reinsurance, leaving the field of insurance proper to the private sector. We further recommend that the Export Development
Corporation serve as the insurer of last resort to close any gaps left by the private sector in the supply of export credit insurance.
That is entirely within the philosophy as posed by the Opposition, and as was stated during the debate on this particular Bill. The Minister may look startled about this, but this is a fact. I quote the next recommendation. It reads:
We recommend that the Export Development Corporation continue to provide direct financing for Canadian sales abroad when there is reason to believe that the private sector is unable to provide the required credits. Public financing should be made available only under terms and conditions commensurable with the risks involved and the costs of such assistance-including the opportunity cost of the funds used-except in those cases where it is deemed necessary to take into consideration the export-support programs of other countries.
This means that the Export Development Corporation would partially withdraw from direct export financing, except when a credit gap is found. This has always existed. I remember many years ago one of the first big breakthroughs in selling railway engines on the world market came between Canada and Mexico. Mexico did not discover any oil. Mexico was a poor country. It needed railway rolling stock and, frankly we needed a good, healthy, productive spurt in the locomotive manufacturing field. This was done with government financing with long-term low interest rates. There was a political element. There is no doubt about that. But, my goodness, it was an economic shot in the arm for both countries and, therefore, it was an activity which was worthy.
That is provided for in the Export Development Act. I believe it is $5 billion or $7 billion now as a result of the amendments, with which the Government of Canada can make direct loans or participate in the financing directly rather than through the corporation.
I quote the following from the next recommendation:
We further recommend that the Export Development Corporation's gradual withdrawal from most direct-lending activities be accompanied by an increased concentration of its efforts in the field of credit insurance and bank guarantees. The Corporation should also stand ready to provide refinancing facilities for private lending institutions engaged in export finance.
That is precisely what a government agency of this kind should be doing in the type of economy we want here in Canada. I have already seen some efforts in this field.
I would like to talk about a brief which was submitted to the Science Council of Canada by the Royal Bank with regard to counter trade, which is a new phenomenon. Counter trade means swapping or barter. For example, if country A wishes to buy from country B, it is on condition that country B may buy from country C, which in turn, will buy something else from country A. It is all a lock-up deal, and that has to be financed. 1 cannot say a lot of Canadian banks, but certainly the Royal Bank, which spoke about this in its brief of May of 1983, said that this is a phenomenon which Canadian business cannot ignore, nor can the Canadian Government. There is one recommendation made that there be, in the section of international trade in External Affairs, a desk designed to deal strictly with counter trade. If we ignore recommendations of this kind, Mr. Speaker, we do so at our own peril.
I have read the last of the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada. I hope I have done so on a positive basis.
September 27, 1983

1 would like to re-emphasize again what was said about counter trade. A classic example, perhaps, is Indonesia. It is perhaps the one which is most widely known among Canadians. By the counter purchase policy instituted in January, 1982, as a means of increasing Indonesia's non-oil exports, foreign companies now tendering on government-funded contracts are required to purchase non-oil, non-gas goods equivalent in value to the contract in the event their bid is accepted.
We in Government have been told time and time again about the necessity for the Canadian business community, and Canada as a whole, to get involved in that North-South trade, so-called, with the Third World countries. The economies of those people are in a precarious state. They do not have a great deal of money lying free to finance the deficits they have in trade. Therefore, this counterbalance, this counter trade practice, has grown up. It is understandable and we have to get involved. The faster we do so, the better, and not only through our private institutions. Not only must private businessman wake up to it, but government must also wake up to it, not next year or the year after, but now. I hope that in the next committee meeting on Bill C-152 the Ministers in question are going to be asked what they are doing about counter trade.

Mr. Speaker, my question to the Hon. Member is as follows: with reference to the question of competition in which EDC might be involved with the private sector, would the hon. gentleman indicate to me whether he has any knowledge, first of all, of any private sector corporation, which is in the export insurance business, which has at any time complained to him or, indeed, has launched a complaint relating to the activities of the EDC?

Mr. Speaker, I have heard rumours of some complaints. Some Hon. Members have raised the question. But 1 have never personally received any complaint with regard to the field of insurance. I do know some of the banks are acting, more recently, in conjunction with EDC on a shared basis, and that is to be encouraged. As to the insurance, I would say this, in fairness, that I believe EDC scared them all out of the field years ago. It has become a state monopoly. That is why I believe the Economic Council of Canada has said, "This state organization must desist from what amounts to intervention by the state which has existed for some time and let the others in."

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman, being very knowledgeable in this field, knows very well the areas to which we are directing our exports. Does he not recognize that the level of risk there is regarding the financing of any export items creates substantial difficulty, especially in today's financial environment, in finding private sector companies that are ready to assume that high level of risk?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am aware of that. On the other hand, I do not think I would like to express it that way. I would much prefer to take a positive approach and say that we have a degree of trust in those people with whom we trade. We
Export Development Act
do not approach them on the basis of high insurance contracts which are an immediate telegraph to others that frankly we will sell to them but we do not trust them very much. That to me is the reaction if it becomes known that the rate charged for an insurance policy is as high as the market will bear.
I think there is room for improvement here. While there have been some difficult times, in the end you will find that if your prime seller, the Canadian businessman, has been on his toes and has a proper contract, the calls on insurance will be much smaller than might be feared.

Mr. Speaker, regarding EDCs involvement in export financing, the Hon. Member has recognized that there has been an increased level of co-operation between the conventional lending institutions and the EDC. Has the hon. gentleman been approached by any of the conventional financing institutions decrying the role of the EDC in export financing or at any time criticizing or claiming that EDC was denying them access to financial returns as a result of its involvement in export financing?

I must say, Mr. Speaker, that personally I have never received any reports. I have read of some representations made by newspaper columnists, presumably expert in the field, suggesting that the financial institutions of Canada had finally decided to, well, go somewhere else because, frankly, competition from the EDC was too severe, the profits to be made were not commensurate with the risk and activity. In the same way, the life insurance companies got shooed out of the house mortgage field some years ago. When I was building my first house and practising law, there was not a bank in this field, there were a few trust companies, and Central Mortgage and Housing only went into larger apartments or limited dividend projects. The rest was done by the NHA with the life insurance companies and some trust companies.
However, and I trust I will end on a positive note, I am hoping we will see that more of the banks, particularly those which have developed over the past five to eight years in the international field and which have taken advantage of the anticipated creation of the B-series banks here in Canada on a reciprocal basis, will get involved. They have learned a great deal more about international financing. They have learned how to work in those markets, and they are there for that particular purpose. I hope that as a result of their activities they will get into a great deal more financing of Canada's exports rather than recourse being made to the EDC on all occasions.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), put on the record many, many times that with a staff of 600 less than 100 applications for financing were processed during the whole year at the EDC. Therefore, the market demand cannot be that great. More and more is being handled, I think, by some of the charter banks, and certainly if the banks are the people who are drawing to our attention the counter trade, that means that they are involved.

September 27, 1983
Export Development Act

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has recognized that there are occasions where international transactions occasion extremely high risk with very low returns, and that creates an environment that is not very attractive to the private sector. In that context, and in view of the fact that there is increasing demand for participation in the export market where this particular environment is to be found, namely high risk and low return, does he not see that there is a need for greater involvement of agencies such as the EDC, to go into areas where the private sector fears to tread?

Well, Mr. Speaker, I will say this much. Having been in this House at the time the EDC or its predecessor was established, I am quite well aware of the compelling reasons at the time. I supported the establishment of the EDC and, yes, there is a place for it. Having said that, I say that its present role should not remain writ on stone, and it would be more in keeping with the need for expanding Canadian trade for it to go more into re-insurance, as the financial backer of last resort, and the encouragement of more participation by private financial institutions. Not only those which operate from Canada, but, as you may know, some 65 foreign banks have established branches here in Canada and they have connections abroad. I would not want these foreign banks to act as bird dogs for business for their home banks.
Now that the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) has come into the House, possibly he would like to say something to us about this question of counter trade, unless my time has expired. We hope the Minister of State for International Trade will give us some learned discourse on the subject of counter trade.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. On the last point made by the Hon. Member for Edmonton West, the Minister of State for International Trade is considered to have spoken because he was the mover of the motion now being debated. He was the prime mover. It was moved on his behalf. Technically he has spoken. He can only speak again with the unanimous consent of the House. I hope that is clear, if he wishes to speak. Debate?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) ended his last remarks on a somewhat complimentary basis, with qualifications however. I too could perhaps start my remarks in a somewhat complimentary fashion, but I might not end on such a complimentary note.
We should now be aware, at this point in the debate on Bill C-110, that after perhaps one of the longest report stage debates on a matter of principle, the Progressive Conservative Party was able to gain substantial concessions toward parliamentary accountability in the Export Development Corporation Bill known as Bill C-110. The authorized capital of the corporation formerly determined its borrowing capacity. In the future, the corporation's borrowing capacity will be limited to ten times its paid-in capital and its retained earnings. The
authorized capital of some $2 billion requested by the Government was reduced, because of long debate, to $1.5 billion. This, in effect, reduces the possible borrowing from $20 billion to $15 billion. In future, the corporation will be required to present its annual report and its financial statements to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for examination, something that has been long overdue. Once again, accountability has been strengthened. Lastly, the Government's right to take up loans and guarantees not appropriate to the EDC's activities has been reduced from $20 billion to $13 billion. That will not answer all of our concerns, but it will some of them, which, in turn, would justify the need for extended debate on the Bill.
There could be no doubt about the difference in approach to government financing that exists between the Progressive Conservative Party and the Liberal Party of Canada. The Progressive Conservative Party believes very strongly in the principle of accountability and control. The Liberal Party, or the governing Party today, believes that the tax dollars of Canadians and their descendants are the property of the Government to do with as it pleases, with as little reference to Parliament and to outside consultation as it can get away with being made possible through legislation. In other words, it is circumventing the responsibility of Parliament or Government to the electors who require representation here in Ottawa.
Bill C-110 has two major thrusts. But before I proceed, and to throw some perspective on the seriousness of the Bill, I must go back a few days in the debate to a statement made by the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens). I wish to quote him directly because it does indicate the seriousness of the matter at hand. As quoted from page 27439 of Hansard, he said:
Let me put it into perspective, if I may. When it comes to the question of whether we are crowding or somehow being unfair to EDC when it requests a $60 billion authorization, let us not forget that as of December 31, 1982 the total corporate and Government lending activities, the total assets of the EDC, were $6.5 billion. That is the total amount it expended as at the end of 1982. It is asking for authorization to make it ten-fold bigger compared with its total assets at the end of the last year of roughly $6.5 billion.
The first major thrust with which we are dealing in Bill C-110 is to expand the operational capacity of the Export Development Corporation, more commonly referred to as the EDC. In so doing, the Government seeks to expand the borrowing capacity of the corporation without need for further reference to Parliament and without need for further paid-in capital. The Government also seeks to increase the amount of high risk or bad business transactions that the Cabinet may approve, originally from $3.5 billion to $10 billion, but now because of changes, from $3.5 billion to $7 billion in the case of insurance. Originally it had requested from $2.5 billion to $10 billion in the case of loans and loan guarantees and now, through debate, that has been reduced to $6 billion. Any losses made under such circumstances are paid from the Consolidated Revenue Fund without future reference to Parliament.
The second major thrust of Bill C-l 10 is to alter the current structure and powers of the board of directors. We will refer to some specific problems in that area. The number of directors
September 27, 1983

increases from 12 to 15, and the requirement that six of the directors be public servants has been dropped. This does not go far enough toward ensuring adequate private sector participation on the board. If the Government so desired, it could appoint no one at all from the private sector. Therefore, I think it fair to say that the Export Development Corporation is not truly accountable to Parliament.
We must consider one specific, glaring example of lack of accountability and the concern involving those who might lobby the financial involvement of Government by again referring to page 27440 of Hansard for September 23, when the Hon. Member for York-Peel, in discussing the lending of money by EDC to a company on whose board sat the Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer, stated:
By sheer coincidence, we find on the board of Bombardier Inc. the Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer, P.C., Q.C. When I noticed that, it rang a bell. That chap used to sit across the aisle, shoulder to shoulder with many of these fellows who are attempting so poorly to govern the country at the present time. As we know, the same Jean-Pierre Goyer is Vice-Chairman of Canadair Inc ... . That company, on the Government's own admission, has blown $1.4 billion of taxpayers' funds. Here we have another company getting the benefit of $970 million worth of financing through the Export Development Corporation, and there is a common Liberal link, Jean-Pierre Goyer ... included in the Bombardier financing through the Export Development Corporation was a sale to the almost defunct New York Transit Authority. If we read the same statistical review, we find that the United States Metropolitan Transportation Authority of New York got two cracks at the Canadian public purse. Directly from EDC it received $294,912,000. The Government stepped in with another $626,688,000. Isn't that nice! Talk about a milk cow! It was so blatant in the United States that the U.S. Commerce Department instituted an action in that country, pointing out that in its opinion the Canadian Government had provided a subsidy amounting to $167,225 for each subway car proposed to be sold to the Transit Authority of New York.
Can you believe that this Government, which denies financing to help commuters get to work in Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver, is willing to subsidize authorities in New York to help workers there get to and from work through a company which happens to have a very friendly director on this board.
He is the already referred to as the Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer, PC, QC. If that does not indicate without question in the minds of those here in the House of Commons a necessity for accountability of the EDC to Parliament, I do not know what will.
The EDC does not have its spending adequately scrutinized here in Parliament. It is not required to table an operating budget, a capital budget or information on the size of its payroll. It may borrow money in the name of Canadian taxpayers, their children and their children's children without seeking parliamentary authority to do just that. But for anyone who has paid attention to the Government's operations and expenditures over the years, this comes as relatively no surprise.
The expansion of Government intervention and the erosion of accountability was accurately reported in 1979 by the Auditor General of Canada, James J. Macdonell. His reports were based upon the findings of four Government-wide studies, each on a different aspect of financial management, control and accountability and each involving upwards of 100,000 hours of professional analysis and study. In terms of size and
Export Development Act
scope, each study could easily in itself be equated to a royal commission. His findings are as important today as they were back in 1979. The conclusions were straightforward and identifiable: control of the public purse had been lost in this country. An attitude permeated the bureaucracy that somehow the taxpayer was accountable to Government.
In 1978, a report to the House of Commons by Macdonell offered these comments on the ballooning and its impact on effective management. I must quote from two paragraphs of that report as follows:
If our findings are an indictment of anything, it is of the system which apparently puts more emphasis on developing policy initiatives and new programs, than on the principles and well-established practices of economical, efficient and effective resource management.
He went on to state:
Operating in a climate which seemed to provide reasonably easy access to a bottomless public purse ... it is not surprising that few Brownie points were available for managers who displayed frugality, let alone parsimony, in spending public funds and bringing in an effective program on schedule and below budget.
It is indeed deplorable that the insight and intelligence of J. J. Macdonell was wasted on a Government that, rather than heeding his warning, increased its interference in the economy and continued to expand at unprecedented rates.
The question of increasing the budget of yet another Crown corporation over which we have no control is absolutely deplorable. I am reminded of a book entitled "The Disease of Government", written by Professor H. S. Ferns of Birmingham, England, who suggests that:
As a result of sustained government intervention in the economy and the creation of regulatory planning and operative government industrial institutions, ... the end of market economies is now in sight... Governments, to be effective as agencies of social co-operation, have to define and limit their role in the community; otherwise governments are a source of confusion, disorder, and other massive evils ... The need to limit the power of governments in the interest of liberty and peace is now universal.
This is exactly why the Progressive Conservative Party is opposing Bill C-l 10, which would increase to $44.5 billion the amount of money that the EDC can borrow, lend and insure without adequate parliamentary control. This Party speaks for the interests of all Canadian taxpayers who no longer want to be misled and confused about Government spending. They like to see government run somewhat like a business, accountable to those who have their money invested.
In the words of a former U.S. Treasury Secretary, William Simon:
-people must be taught to start calling for a rollback of the bureaucracy, where nothing will be lost but strangling regulation and where gains will always take the form of liberty, productivity and jobs.
Today we are indeed forced to witness a disease of Government, and it is a malady which, if allowed to go unchecked, will not be susceptible to cure.
Let me quote from Hansard of September 23, at page 27442. This was said by the Hon. Member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates):
We are making an argument that is as old as democracy itself-that there has to be accountability by the Government for the money it extracts from the taxpayers of Canada and then spends.

September 27, 1983
Export Development Act
As we have gone through debate on Bill C-l 10, speaker after speaker has given us many examples of the tremendous proliferation of Crown corporations and their belief that they are sacred and unassailable and that it is impossible to examine their activities.
Only this week I was shocked to see that the Chairman of the CNR, Jack Horner a former Member of the House and one who stood on many occasions to talk about accountability and the requirement to have Members on the Treasury benches account to us for the money spent, supposedly on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada-was reported as saying that he did not believe the Auditor General should audit the books of the CNR.
That is exactly what we are saying here in the House during this debate. That is what the Auditor General should be permitted to do.
Seven years ago, the Auditor General noted that in the majority of Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control is weak and ineffective. Moreover, co-ordination and guidance by central Government agencies of financial management and control practices in these Crown corporations are virtually non-existent.
1 do not see anything different being said in my remarks today and the remarks of the Auditor General than was said by Jack Horner who, now in his capacity as Chairman of the CNR, feels that auditing by the Auditor General should not occur.
It is a shame that we have to live with such inconsistencies on the record. The time for reports and discussion has passed. The time has come for meaningful action to be taken to increase the accountability and control of Crown corporations.
The EDC is proof positive that the current Government has, for many years, been unwilling to listen to the Auditor General, Members of Parliament on both sides and most important, the individual Canadian taxpayer.
It has been completely unresponsive to the needs and aspirations of the voters. Canadians are demanding cost effectiveness in Government to act as an inspiration for recovery and hope. Instead, we see a Government which continues to expand and spend money without regard for costs.
Last Wednesday, we listened to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek), expound on the virtues of increased trade and its ability to increase jobs. We are all aware of the benefits of export development, yet this Government seems to feel that only it is capable of making important decisions regarding trade.
The Economic council, in its report, entitled "Intervention and Efficiency", noted this fact on page 51:
Canada is perhaps the country with the least private-sector participation in export financing decisions. The Governments of most other industrial nations encourage bank participation in this area, more so than does the Government of Canada. In six of the industrialized countries examined, the supply of primary financing is left completely in the hands of the private sector, which may, however resort to public rediscounting facilities. In most of the 17 countries studied, the negotiations for granting export credit are also left to the private sector. This is not the case in Canada, where direct negotiations take place between the EDC and the foreign buyer. When the banks are invited to participate jointly with the EDC in long-term financing, they often complain of being denied access to all the information and to the negotiations, and of being presented with ready-made proposals.
This was according to a report of the Economic Council of Canada entitled, "Intervention and Efficiency". The private sector must participate more in the decisionmaking process of the EDC. However, Liberals believe that the bureaucrats who govern most govern best. It is imperative that the Export Development Corporation be governed by a disciplined, costconscious board of directors. The Government has a responsibility to Parliament and to the people of Canada to ensure that the public purse is not treated as a bottomless pit.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there Hon. Members who are rising to ask questions or to make comments? If there are none, the Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker).

Mr. Speaker, we are drawing to the close of another Bill, Bill C-l 10, and once again I rise to indicate that it reflects the fundamental problems of process in the House of Commons and the rules by which we govern ourselves.
Some two years ago this Bill was started. It is now getting through. I agree with anyone who says that the process takes too long. Two years is much too long for the passage of Bill C-l 10. But that begs a question. It is not just simple Opposition intransigence which is trying to stop the Bill. There were very good, honest and legitimate reasons to stop it, just as there were good and honest reasons for the Government to want to get a Bill amending the EDC through Parliament. Somehow between those two forces we have a stand-off at high noon. The problem mainly goes back to process and our views on what the House is all about. Certainly some of the delay resulted from Government priority. It brought forth many other Bills which took a lot of House time to get through. It was a question of the Cabinet as the executive of the nation setting its priorities as to what Bills it wanted. Certainly the House, and particularly the Opposition, canmnot be blamed for that. The Government is entitled to set its own rules.
I suppose the main reason for the opposition, as indicated by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), was accountability. Since the Second World War over 400 Crown corporations have been established. If we did in all their subsidiaries, the figure would be much larger. The question arises as to how a democratic society controls Crown corporations. Most of the board members and appointments to Crown corporations are made by the executive. This has caused a sub-government tied into the main executive, the Cabinet. We see a close relationship between Crown corporations and Government departments, which has resulted in a lack of accountability for taxpayers' dollars.
We must always remember that our primary objective as elected officials is to protect the dollar which comes out of our pockets as citizens and, because of the deficits which have built up, will come out of the pockets of our children and grandchildren. Ordinary Canadians can quite properly criticize us for not developing a process and mechanism to protect their dollars. For every dollar a private citizen cannot decide to
September 27, 1983

spend, there is a dollar in the hands of the Government which it decides to spend, at the expense of the work, effort and sweat of ordinary citizens. That is principle 1 am against.
Millions and millions of individual decisions by ordinary Canadians on how to spend their own dollars would lead to a much wiser result than those dollars being taxed away and spent by a few men and women of whatever political stripe. When we believe that an executive can make better decisions than ordinary Canadians, we are wrong. If we continue the way we are, we will return to the pre-1750s when there really was state capitalism in the form of a monarchy and a tightly knit group of advisers and counsellors. Essentially that is what we are returning today. We have a duty to oppose it today just as people fought and indeed gave their lives in the 1700s for the right to make their own decisions, which of course was primarily the right to property.
Not only is there the issue of accountability. There is also the issue of freedom of information and the legitimate role of Parliament versus bureaucracy. The Bill before us reflects once again how many Bills come through the bureaucratic process to Parliament. We all know the charts that show how an idea about something which needs to be done progresses through the bureaucracy. There is a huge chart indicating the Departments through which each Bill has to go. There are arrows going each way, whether it be to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Finance or Treasury Board. The arrows go both ways indicating a dialogue, but in the far right-hand corner of the chart there is a little tiny box marked "Parliament". There is an arrow into it and there is an arrow out the other side. It is the job of the executive to get it through Parliament with no amendments. That is what we stand here resisting.
I believe Government Members should be seeing this matter from a different perspective as well. If a Bill has not originated with one of us as Parliamentarians but has come through the bureaucracy, then we must check that bureaucracy, which is becoming increasingly larger. They are individually fine people, but collectively they have taken on a power which has subsumed the power of the House. Indeed, Government backbenchers should play a much more critical role in the consideration of legislation which comes before us. This Bill is a particular example.
Two years ago the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) brought forward three amendments which would have made the Bill acceptable. It was similar to the constitutional package which the Government could have had by Christmas of the year it was brought in, if it would have accepted one amendment. The Government would not accept the amendment, so we fought for months and months, causing enormous division in the country. These three amendments were reasonable in themselves. This Bill could have been law for two years.
What were the amendments? Of course, the first one concerned more private individuals on the board of directors rather than public servants appointed by the executive or the
Export Development Act
Cabinet. The second concerned financial disclosure, especially of the interest rate subsidies used. The reason these should be known is that every time some dimension of an industry is subsidized, we are really delaying a problem which ultimately surfaces and has to be dealt with. But when it has to be faced ultimately, the problems are ten times worse and the agony is great indeed. It is better to face it at the beginning. Why do we not have that information up front so that we can deal with it and everyone can operate above board? Then there would be no financial foolishness or skullduggery under the table. Of course, the third amendment indicated that major commitments or appropriations by EDC should come before Parliament. My original thesis was that the primary role of individual Members of Parliament was that of a financial watchdog. If we accept that, then surely this amendment was a reasonable one.
Had the Government accepted the amendments of the Hon. Member for Calgary South, the Bill would already be two years old and we would have had more time to direct our energy and effort as Members to some of the other major problems in the country rather than fight over the principles of accountability, freedom of information and the role of Parliament. While we fight for what we believe and while the Government continues to fight for secrecy and Government by executive fiat without any responsibility to the House, the nation is literally being destroyed. We stand here fiddling while Rome burns, while Canada is being destroyed.
With a simple change of the rules of the House, we could make it that votes against the Government on ordinary pieces of legislation would not result in the Government falling and having to call an election. We have often argued in the House that it is only on the budget, the Throne Speech and major pieces of critical policy legislation that the Government would declare a question of confidence. On ordinary pieces of legislation such as an amendment to this statute or the Farm Credit Corporation, the bulk of which come out of the bureaucracy, backbenchers on both sides in the House and in committee should be able to take a critical look at that legislation. If we do not like it, we vote it down and the Cabinet Minister would say, "Fine, ladies and gentlemen, you do not like it, we will take it back and re-work it." We could do that. We do not need to have responsible Government on ordinary pieces of legislation, particularly in the twentieth century when legislation is much more significant and there are literally thousands of pieces of legislation on the books.
While we fiddle, the country is being destroyed. As the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) said, our over-all trade has gone down from 5 per cent to 3 per cent. In manufactured products, it has dropped from 4 per cent to 2 per cent. Had we retained our original 5 per cent and 4 per cent, we would have had 50 per cent fewer people unemployed than we do today. Think of that in terms of the unemployment insurance dollars and the welfare dollars that would be saved. With another 750,000 people working, tax revenues would be so much greater. The deficit would be smaller.

September 27, 1983
Export Development Act
I have argued about the effects of the deficit. Just as night follows day, deficits lead to inflation, which, in turn, leads to high interest rates, which, in turn, leads to a collapse such as we are experiencing today. There is an adjustment factor that takes place when nations have huge deficits such as we now have. We have between 1.5 million and 2 million people unemployed.
If we had 50 per cent fewer people unemployed, the extra tax revenue would have permitted the Government to do so much more. It would not be in the marketplace borrowing all the money. There would have been more capital that people would have had to put into businesses because there would be nowhere else to invest it in terms of government.
The way it is today, people can sit back and take absolutely no risk whatsoever. They can lend to their Government and get an enormous rate of return. We had a classic example a couple of years ago where people got 19.5 per cent. If two years ago you had a million dollars to invest and lent it to the Government, you would have received an income of $195,000 without taking one scintilla of risk. If the Government had not been demanding the money and competing, that money would have had to be put into the marketplace. It is true there would have been a risk, but we would have seen the building of plants and the creation of jobs. Therefore, we might have had even less unemployment.
Two years later the original amendments have not been accepted. Other amendments have been brought forth, lately the amendments which were accepted which dealt with the lending capacity of the corporation and automatic reference to a standing committee, a change in the borrowing arrangements restricting it to ten times paid-up capital. Over-all, as I said earlier, the basis of our objection is accountability. At third reading, when we are to look at the Bill in principle as amended, do we still have outstanding issues that have not been dealt with? 1 submit we do. Therefore, the problems will continue with respect to this and other corporations. We will continue to waste enormous amounts of time in the House as well as human vitality and energy which could be put to positive use building a greater nation rather than spinning our wheels.
The first issue is whether the Export Development Corporation could be lending money directly or whether it should have an insurance function. We have read the reports and the original statute. Prior to 1970, the EDC was an insurance agency. Since then it has been lending money. As the Economic Council points out, if the EDC were to return to an insurance principle, it would get a much bigger bang for its buck. By guaranteeing money, you would put out a little bit of money in terms of insurance coverage. That would go a lot farther than lending an actual sum of money to one corporation.
The second issue has, to a certain extent, been dealt with in the Bill. It deals with the bureaucratic nature of the corporation. I would like to ask EDC why it took over 600 people to process 100 applications last year. There may be a perfectly
rational answer. They may be able to show that everybody put in a full day's labour and that it was valuable to the country.
However, if there is padding and too many people, that makes the corporation look inefficient. It also tends to reduce morale in the corporation. As well, it ties up people with all sorts of vitality and experience. They may be able to go to another area of government or another corporation which could use those people in terms of making applications to EDC. They would understand the internal nature of the corporation and government itself. We need to look at the red tape, the expense and the cumbersome nature of the applications.
The third issue is the whole process where, for some reason or other, the bulk of the corporation money is going to a very restricted number of corporation. Some of our Members talked about Atomic Energy of Canada, a Crown corporation, and de Havilland Aircraft, another Crown corporation. If it is the Government's intention that its own Crown corporations are to get priority and have access to public tax dollars indirectly through the corporation rather than through direct Government appropriations, Government purchases of shares or straight Government loans, why do we not face that question? Why do we pay 600 people to operate the EDC and run money into Crown corporations when we would not need anybody to do that if we run it through departmental loans or Government investment in equity? 1 wonder if the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) would rise and give his views on that.
The fifth issue which has not been dealt with to my satisfaction in trying to follow these issues, together with other issues that come before us, is the whole question of concessionary finance where we subsidize interest rates on loans to other countries so that those countries can buy goods from Canada, which creates employment. The effect is that the deficit continues to get larger. These deficits in themselves are much more dangerous on a long term than the problems they are trying to solve. The Government says that it is better than we lend it the money and subsidize it so that Canadians are employed because if Canadians are employed, they are not rioting in the streets. It does not need to be that way because I think one can always go to the people and explain that the situation is that we are either priced out of the market, because of our northern climate where it takes too much heat to grow plants and therefore we must reduce our fuel taxes, or perhaps because our labourers are demanding too much in wages. Labourers would be prepared to work for less if the costs of their loans and mortgages were lower, because it is all relative. If we increase the deficit and therefore interest rates, the ordinary labourer will, quite properly, ask for more money to meet his day-to-day needs. If we do not increase the deficit and keep all those expenses down, then that labourer does not have to ask for more money. It does not have to be the way it is now.
