I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are rising to point out that my time has expired. 1 could go on to many other issues, but 1 will leave it at that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there Elon. Members seeking to ask questions or make comments at this time? If there are none, the Chair recognizes the Elon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor).

Mr. Speaker, this is the fourth time that 1 have endeavoured to speak to this particular Bill. The Bill is becoming more familiar to me each time 1 speak.
1 am much happier with the Bill as it is now than 1 was when I spoke previously. At that time, the Bill was bad in a number of respects, particularly on the issue of accountability. The Export Development Corporation had been given the power to borrow $2 billion and then had been given the power to multiply that by ten to borrow $20 billion without reference to the Parliament of Canada. That is the part that we were seriously concerned about.
I heard an Hon. Member today question why this debate had gone on for so long. That is the very reason. This is an important aspect of parliamentary democracy. If we lose accountability and the control of the public purse, we do not have a parliamentary democracy of the kind spoken about by the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Great Britain yesterday. Parliament must take responsibility. When that happens, we have proper representation.
As I mentioned on one other occasion, there was a time when the representation was true. When Parliament first began, everybody went to the site of Parliament. Everybody was present. Each person voted the way he felt he should vote. That was true democracy. As society and the population grew, that became impossible, so we devised a scheme whereby representatives went to Parliament to represent 5,500 people, 10,000 people, and today there are Members of the House who represent more than 100,000 people.
As the population grows, it becomes difficult to reflect the thinking of the greatest possible majority in a riding, but that is the responsibility of the Member. He can do that through a number of means. He can stand for certain principles at election time, and if people elect him they expect him to uphold those principles. He can hold a series of public meetings to secure the wishes of his constituents, as indeed I did when discussing the Crow Bill. People turned out in large numbers at five meetings that were held in my riding. The people who were there were a cross-section of the country. There were farmers, businessmen, hog producers, cattle producers, grain growers and processors. They indicated how they wanted their elected representative to vote in the House of Commons. Almost unanimously they wanted their representative to vote for the freedom of choice which is the basis of our democracy.
Export Development Act
When our forefathers went West seeking land, they went West with determination. They had little money but strong backs. They had little more than the clothes on their backs, but they were determined to build a heritage. They were determined to develop something of which their children could be proud. Among those things which they were determined to develop was accountability. A father bought a farm and his children worked. Accountability was learned in the farmstead. So it was in the mining camps. We were taught that we had to be accountable.
I remember a time when 1 received 25 cents a day for looking after my neighbour's cows. 1 took the cows up the hill at seven in the morning and I went to get them at six o clock at night when 1 got home from school. I received 25 cents a day for that. 1 remember my mother saying to me that that came to $1.75 a week and that I must be accountable for that money. She asked me what 1 was going to do with it in ten weeks. I had to be accountable. That is the lesson that Government officials must learn.
To a considerable degree, we now have accountability in this Bill. There is not as much accountability as we would like to see, but there is now much more accountability than there was before. But what about all the other corporations? What about the Government itself? We want accountability in the Parliament of the country. We are not in Moscow where the Government can do what it likes without the knowledge of the people. That Government simply tells the people what is good for them. That is not what we want in Canada.
We want the Members of a democratic Parliament to reflect to the greatest possible degree the thinking of the people who sent them to Parliament. We want the Government to include that thinking in its administration, in its policies and in its laws to the greatest possible degree. That is democracy. We have gotten far away from that.
Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that the people of the country, whether they live in P.E.I., Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, the Yukon, the Northwest Territories or Indian reservations, would have favoured seeing the country go into debt by spending more than it made this year, by spending $31 billion more than it takes in? Not on your life, Mr. Speaker.
I represent three Indian reservations and 1 have met with the band councils. 1 have learned to respect our Indian people. Our Indian people are not illiterate, as some people think. They are business people. I remember the time the Indians I represent came to me and said: "How can we be accountable when we apply for a grant first thing in the spring in order to put in a sewer system on our reserve, we get the money in October; and then the Government says we have to spend it now or we lose the money?" Rather than lose the money, they try to spend it in October. What happens then? They are putting in sewer lines in frosty conditions, the worst possible time to put in a sewer system. In the west, snow often falls in the middle of October. Sometimes the snow comes before that, but I have seen pretty severe winters starting on October 15.

September 27, 1983
Export Development Act
Here they were trying to put sewer lines in in November. That is a waste of public money.
One of the Indian band councillors from the Blackfoot Reserve said that they were wasting the money but they have to do it. The Government told them they had to do it. That is not accountability on the part of the Government, Mr. Speaker. Our Indian people had no choice. They had to do it or else lose the money entirely and be told the following year that they had lost their chance.
Accountability does not exist when an Indian reservation applies for a grant in the spring and they get it in October. Surely it does not take months to go over these papers. Sometimes I write letters to Ministers of the Government and I get an answer back within a week. Other times I get an answer back three months later. Is that doing the job? I have been a Minister and I have had some heavy portfolios. At one time I was responsible for the motor vehicle branch, the Department of Highways, the research council, the licensing of drivers and the cancellation of licences for drunk drivers, et cetera. It was a tremendous load. As well, I was responsible for the telephone system of Alberta. I know the many hours of work that are involved, Mr. Speaker, but people did not have to wait three months for a reply to letters. If the letters piled up I worked until the early hours of the morning, and that is what Ministers should do. Of course, I understand there is a limit, but surely three, four or five months' delay on a reply is no way to run a public business. That is not accountability.
The whole matter of accountability is what is involved here, Mr. Speaker. Due to the tremendous work of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and others who helped him, we have gained that to some extent in this Bill. The Government finally gave in, and now will be accountable for this particular corporation, but what about all the others and the Ministries? They should all be accountable if we are to have anything like a democracy. I hope that now that the Bill is just about ready to go to the Senate, we will be able to get results from our international trade and export market.
I should like to tell the House of an incident that really hurt me, Mr. Speaker. In the City of Drumheller we were close to getting an industry with world-wide connections, but then the Government refused to give the last grant that was required. They may never have had to call on the guarantee, but they refused that guarantee, and today the company has gone into receivership. About 200 people were thrown out of work. When I go through the west part of Drumheller, I see machines sitting idle. That industry could have provided 150 families with a living and could have been exporting machines, but the Federal Business Development Bank would not give a guarantee so that the program could go into the final stages.
One machine the company manufactured was a 139 cultivator and the Prasko seeder which could have been sent to Third World countries if a guarantee had been provided. The Prasko air seeder is a tremendous innovation and has all kinds of
potential. All the research had been carried out, but in the final stages, when the cash flow was needed, it was not available. The bank would not take a chance that it might not succeed but, rather, made sure that it did not succeed, and the company went into receivership. It also made the chisel plow. These implements could have been used all around the world and could have provided work for 150 or more people. Welders from all over Canada could have been given work instead of being put on the unemployment rolls. Financial institutions would not go along with the proposal, however, and had to have their money then and there. The Government would not give any guarantee, so the plant went under. Today, in Drumheller that site sits cold and lonely, hundreds of Prasko seeders in the yard and scores of people drawing unemployment insurance. It is no wonder the Unemployment Insurance Fund is disappearing, Mr. Speaker. The only way to keep the fund functioning is to have more and more people working. The people who worked at the Prasko plant put their whole life's savings into running it, but the Government would not take a chance. But the Government took a chance with Imperial Oil to the tune of $30 billion. It is no wonder there are two million people unemployed. There is no incentive for people to invest their money, either. If we invest our money, then we create jobs. Perhaps only one or two people would be hired to start with, but any business can expand.
Another thing that hurts us is the capital gains tax. In Turner Valley a man showed me an empty lot with a garage beside it which he owned. He wanted to expand, and he said to me, If you think I want to do that for any blinkety blankety Government, you are crazy. I will do it for my family. I will work 24 hours a day for my son and daughter and my wife, but I am not going to work for the Government to grab the money.
I will pay income tax as I go along, but when I die or sell the business 1 do not want to have to pay all over again."
The capital gains tax is unfair. It kills incentive and halts expansion. It is no wonder we have two million people unemployed. There is no incentive to invest in this country anymore.
Just the other day I was on a plane returning to Ottawa. The man in the seat beside me told me that he had money invested in Florida. He said, "The way things are going in this country 1 need a little nest egg for my wife and family if I get ill and cannot work. But the way things are going in this country, I have no faith in the Government." As a result, he is investing his money in another country. The Government is responsible for that attitude, and it is mostly because in so many cases there has not been enough accountability.
In Parliament, we should turn our eyes inward and find out what we are doing wrong. I suggest the first thing we need is what the Hon. Member for Mississauga South fought for so ably in this Bill-accountability and control of the public purse. When industry sees that the Government is paying its own way and not spending money it does not have, then industry will follow suit.
The Bill has been improved greatly, Mr. Speaker. The effort made by all Hon. Members, particularly the effort of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, has been repaid because now
September 27, 1983

there will be some responsibility-unless there is some loophole we have not found yet. I hope that is not so. 1 hope this corporation will become a model for every other corporation, all 300 of them, so that we can eventually change all legislation and make them all responsible to Parliament, which will have the final say in regard to these things.
Parliament should have the final say. Parliament should have the right to control the moneys which are expended. I used the illustration the other day of King John and the Magna Carta. King John was spending wildly for various projects he wanted, not what the people particularly wanted, and when he came back from France one time, he was met by some of the people of Britain. They met him on the field of Runnymede and said to him, "We want you to sign here. We want you to be responsible. We want you to be accountable. We want to have some say in the money you collect and the way in which you spend it." It was a small beginning, but that was the basis of our Parliament today. As the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Great Britain said yesterday, "Accountability, that is the difference between a democracy and a totalitarian state." In a totalitarian state the people have no business knowing what the government is doing. They have no right to know. They cannot gather in Red Square and protest in the way the Canadian people can line up and even sleep on our grounds and protest about something which might eventually save their lives.
1 see you rising, Mr. Speaker. I am just barely getting started, but I recognize the rules. The 20 minutes go pretty fast. I would like just to say in conclusion that 1 hope this Bill will be a model, that this corporation will be accountable to this Parliament, that it will be an example to all other corporations and that we will now start on a new course in this country with government responsible and with the Parliament of Canada having control of the purse strings of the nation.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this last segment of the debate on Bill C-l 10, 1 would first of all like to deal with a number of subjects which have arisen from time to time, namely those of competitiveness and productivity as they affect both our export markets and our ability to lengthen our production lines for our domestic market within Canada. In relating to both competitiveness and productivity, I would like to make some particular reference to the questions of the debt burden, interest rates and inflation which have plagued not only government, but industry, over the last number of years.
The idea espoused by many speakers in this debate so far, that workers have created their inflationary misery through the wage-price spiral, would be funny were the effects not so harsh and tragic for millions of Canadians. Both high interest
Export Development Act
rates and the high rate of inflation can be traced directly to the office door of business. The high inflation which began in the late 1960s came from two main sources, the Viet Nam war

that is some time ago but it is important for us to bear in mind-and a conglomerate merger boom which occurred in both Canada and the United States. That inflation declined during the mid-1970s, but returned with a vengeance in recent years. It is only now beginning to ebb through a deliberately induced recession and depression in many world economies. No one has more successfully induced that depression than has the Government and the business community of Canada.
This inflation is tied to an even higher military expenditure and a merger boom to end all merger booms. The only people to benefit from these trends are corporate shareholders, and 90 per cent of Canadians do not even own one share. Let us first dispose of the idea that government is the only source of inflation. Business and government have been equal partners, but not equal offenders. The federal debt in Canada was virtually unchanged from 1968 to 1973. Until 1978 it grew by 17.5 per cent per year, on average. Corporate debt has grown by 15 per cent to 16 per cent every year since 1968-every year. Government is not blameless, but business has been at it much more steadily and much longer.
Corporations have also the ability to print money. They do it through mergers and takeovers. Company A buys the outstanding shares of Company B, but pays a premium over the usual trading price which has averaged 60 per cent over the last few years. This means that billions of dollars of unproductive debt are added to company balance sheets. And this means, of course, higher prices for both goods and services, and the consumer gets the bill. Increasingly, business does not go to the market for capital, and it has not done so for some time. The so-called "democracy of the marketplace" which many Hon. Members, particularly Conservatives, but many on the other side of the House, still tout as being something real, actually, it is a fairy tale, Mr. Speaker. Business increasingly does not go to the marketplace for its capital for takeovers or for investment. It builds those funds into its own price structure. That amounts to taxation without representation. No one complains when prices reflect the production of goods at a reasonable profit, but when business does not go to the marketplace, and takes it out of largely administered price structures, because of the increasing corporation monopoly control which the larger corporations have gained, it is taxation without representation and there is no other word for it. The democracy of the marketplace in this situation is an absolute myth.
Takeovers in Canada came to $55 billion for 1976 to 1981. This means an additional $20 billion or more in business debt. Mergers are just not productive and there is nothing in the market system to justify them or make them desirable, not the large corporate mergers which we have seen increasingly in recent years. Of course, some of our economic problems are imported from the United States. Its federal debt passed the trillion dollar mark in 1981. However, since 1975 it has spent more than $650 billion on arms. The increase in its massive federal debt is mainly caused by arms expenditures. On that

Export Development Act
point, Mr, Speaker, it is interesting to note that the new Leader of the Conservative Party, its new messiah, has been advocating, along with his caucus colleagues, ever-increasing defence expenditures in Canada, which again will create some of the same kind of problems, albeit on a smaller scale, as has been the case in the United States in the last few years where the Reagan administration has found that its promises just cannot be brought to bear fruit, largely as a result of it. Some of that business has come to Canadian firms, but it is all play money. Billions of these dollars have been pumped into both economies, but there has not been a corresponding increase in goods. This puts great inflationary pressure on prices. There is too much money chasing too few goods, in the classical term. The merger boom has helped raise interest rates through increased competition for large amounts of capital. In other words, the high interest rates which have driven many Canadian small businesses, farms and home owners into bankruptcy, have happened because those very same ordinary Canadians, normally productive, have been forced to foot the bill for corporate mergers. These mergers will in turn make things even worse for them and drive even more of them out of business.
That is the kind of problem we face with the kind of economy we have seen in Canada and in many other countries over the last few years. The myth of a free enterprise society in a country which is rapidly becoming a corporate society and a corporate state is just a myth. It is a fairy tale. As long as the Government, the Official Opposition Party and the people act as if the fairy tale were true, we will continue, I submit, to get deeper and deeper into debt and deeper and deeper into severe trouble, both in our economy and as a society.
Home owners trying to renew their mortgages cannot compete with Seagrams, Dome Petroleum or Petro-Canada. We cannot control inflation in the United States, but we can put our own house in order. If we let companies continue to merge as they wish, we must prohibit them from passing on the additional cost to the public. Let the billions come out of dividends. If shareholders know they will have to pay directly and immediately for their lust to acquire, it might slow them down. That would help bring down both inflation and interest rates. The Government has subsidized the takeover game and we can no longer expect ordinary Canadian wage earners, small business people, farmers and consumers to pay for it.
There has also been a lot of talk during this debate from both sides as to the strategies we must follow. I would like to touch for a few brief moments on some of the strategies we have followed which were endorsed, both implicitly and explicitly by both the Liberal Government and the Conservative Opposition.
What?
Northeast Coal in British Columbia.
What has that got to do with-

That company, again supported by the B.C. Members of the Conservative Party, hand in hand with their Social Credit allies-they do not like to hear the truth, Mr. Speaker. To quote from a recent article in a Canadian Press story-
How about the EDC?

-it says:
On the eve of the formal opening of two more coal mines in western Canada, an independent report has forecast that one or more of the mines now operating or under construction in British Columbia will be forced to close within a few years.
The report, prepared by industry analysts H.N. Halverson Consultants Ltd., nominates as the most likely candidates for closure 'new mines in remote locations'-the Quintette and Bullmoose Mines at the centre of the Northeast Coal project.
We are in the middle, Mr. Speaker, of spending well over $1 billion in public money, not to mention the private money, to create a huge edifice in northeastern British Columbia which is already outdated. The respective Governments were told by some of the top analysts in the field that this was totally outdated before they made the investment.
Another example, Mr. Speaker, was the pre-build pipeline. That was supported by the Liberal Government and the Conservative Opposition. Once again we have to say we told you so, but it would give us a lot more joy to say, "You guys were right and it is working out." But you threw away whatever leverage or bargaining power we had. We are now in a situation, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen: "Don't blame us for gas problems, Americans told". Canadian Ambassador Allan Gotlieb:
-speaking to a luncheon meeting of the American Gas Association in Washington, said the Canadian Government has become concerned at some of the punitive measures being put forward in the U.S. Congress against imports of Canadian natural gas.
Not only was there not an ironclad agreement, not only did we throw away our leverage, not only are we exporting our cheap gas instead of providing the right of way for a pipeline so the Americans can burn their own Arctic gas, the Americans are now saying that because the gas was fixed at a cheap price we are undercutting some of their own gas production and they want to penalize us for that. That is the fault of the Conservative and Liberal Parties, tweedledum and tweedledee.
Oh, oh!
They advocated that as a joint policy, just as they and their friends advocated Northeast Coal.
What has this got to do with EDC?
They are both a flop. Both Parties and both projects are a flop, and they should have known. We do not know anything, of course; we are New Democrats.
Hear, hear!

We are the ones who told them that the oil and gas companies were lying in the early 1970s, and they

said, "Who do you think you are?" "Who does Tommy Douglas think he is?", they asked. Two years later when the whole thing fell apart, they are sitting there red-faced and they cannot understand. They are the biggest bunch of absolute phonies in the world, and that is a polite phrase. I only wish some of the people in the media would read their own newspapers of a few years back.
How about you reading the Bill?

They would realize that while some of us are certainly not infallible, every once in a while we know something about the marketplace that they fail to understand and appreciate, that it is not a fairyland where you can give away what you have, have no bargaining power left, and then have the right to complain because somebody takes you for a ride. We are constantly being taken for a ride. These guys over here, the Conservatives, and those guys over there, the Liberals, have been the drivers who have taken us for that ride into the sorry situation in which we find our economy today.
Who is introducing this Bill?

Maybe the Government wants to atone for its sins. Maybe it is going to turn over a new leaf and behave in a little more accountable and responsible way. But you will pardon us, Mr. Speaker, if we have to see it to believe it. We have been a long time waiting.
While the Conservatives and Liberals have joined in one megaproject boondoggle after another, projects which have collapsed in our faces, most regrettably those of the people of Canada, they have continually neglected over decades and decades and decades the renewable resources of this land, the forest industry in particular. Again, it is many small companies in that industry which need assistance from the EDC and other agencies of Government because they do not have the wherewithal to seek out many of those specialized markets in Europe, the Middle East and other places, in many cases where the purchasing companies are willing to put the capital up front. Those smaller companies, which are lean enough, hungry enough and adaptable enough to be able to cut their product to suit those markets, do not have the facilities to seek those markets out. They need that kind of assistance and require financial assistance in start-up costs, modification costs, so they can meet the markets many of us know are there.
I have had, Mr. Speaker, many examples in my own electoral district, certainly in the adjoining ones, of small private companies which made it during this period when the giants were flopping and failing, the giants which have been traditionally favoured by both the Government and representatives of the Official Opposition whether in Ottawa or the various Provinces. I have seen them make it because they are willing to adapt. They are willing to go out as much as they can with their limited resources, change their production line and their measurements. They will go to metric, imperial or whatever. They will cut one foot, two foot, three foot or whatever is required in order to adapt to the market as it exists. They do not sit back on their fat rumps like a lot of the majors have
Export Development Act
done in the forest industry over the last few years and say, "Come to us". Markets do not just come to you, especially in lean times. They got so used to being big and fat when times were great and they sat back and said, "We are just going to cut for volume. To heck with quality. To heck with having to modify our industrial plant to meet whatever demands are there." So they have collapsed.
If it were just those corporate managers who had to suffer, Mr. Speaker, well, they made the decisions and they have the right to suffer. But there are 300 communities across this country who have suffered terribly from the consequences of their decisions. There are hundreds of thousands of working people and small businesses which provide the machinery and support services those companies traditionally require, and they have been the ones which have had to suffer. Just as the ordinary consumers and farmers and small business people and homeowners of Canada have had to suffer through interest rates and inflation for which corporate mergers and the arms budget in the U.S. were in large part responsible, so are the service industries and small business people in 300 communities across Canada being asked to pay the price once again for decisions that they had no part whatsoever in making.
1 would like to conclude simply by saying that one of the things that we have to address, if we are talking about the nature of the economy we must have if we are to adapt and not serve just some mythical target but the needs of the Canadian people, is to decide whether we want an accountable society with decentralized power-structures where people from all walks of life have a more direct say in governing their communities, their resources and their means of livelihood. In that way they can ensure the decisions made meet their needs and not just self perpetuating corporate managers. Or do we want a society in which an increasingly concentrated and monopolistic corporate big daddy, through its Government agents, be they Liberal or Conservative, decides what is best for him with the interests of the people and the nation as an afterthought? Those are the two choices facing Canadians. It is, fundamentally the choice, represented broadly-though we are not without sin-between the NDP on one side of the argument and the Liberals and Tories on the other. No matter what legislation the Government passes, if it does not decide that it will make the economy work for people rather than have the people work for the economy, it will fall flat on its face. The ordinary people of Canada are the ones who will be continuously asked to pay the price. They have paid enough. It is time the Government gave them a product that was worth it.

Could one imagine what would happen to this country if the NDP did away with all business? It is against business and against profit. What a mess we would have. 1 am glad the Hon. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: 1 hesitate to interrupt the Hon. Member, but I would call to his attention the Bill before us, Bill C-l 10. While there has been some leeway with regard to subject matter, the Hon. Member does appear to be straying a bit.

I hope we will not have a double standard here, Mr. Speaker. There was much talk of investment and where investment is going, and I would like to make some comments. I have figures going back to the time of the prior Government in Manitoba, from 1969 to 1977, concerning the amount of investment that was driven out of the Province, either into Alberta or into the United States. I have also seen the amount of investment money that these people across the way have driven out of this country, in the billions. It is reducing in amount now, because there is nothing else left to go.
I was recently on a trip back to Winnipeg and I had a conversation with a developer. He works out of Winnipeg at Toronto. All his work is in Texas, Louisiana and Florida. That is where all the investment money is going. There will never be any economic recovery in this country as long as we have this Liberal bunch in, I can guarantee that, because they cannot attract investment. All they do is drive it out of the country. I was also reading a recent trade magazine and found that Kentucky advertises itself as being the eleventh Province. It stated, "Come to Kentucky, where profit is not a dirty word." That is what these people have done to this country. I have seen other examples in Manitoba of the New Democratic Party getting into the Chinese food business and what have you, and that folded up also.
The Export Development Corporation is one of the many Crown corporations which has a highly inefficient operation. For example, in 1982 the Export Development Corporation's 613 employees had loan transactions with 62 companies and placed slightly in excess of 900 separate insurance policies. How many banks have ten employees for every loan customer? How many insurance companies in the private sector issue insurance policies at an annual rate of one and one half policies per employee?
The Government makes money on its export insurance coverage, but fails to market the insurance adequately. Only a small handful of corporations received the benefit of the Export Development Corporation's export subsidies. Little is being done to expand this circle. The Export Development Corporation's actual profit last year was $1 million on capital of $691 million, a rate of return of one-tenth of 1 per cent.
To quote from the Economic Council of Canada's report, "Intervention and Efficiency", "Government assistance should be of a temporary nature. But each year, as time goes by, the
names of the firms receiving assistance from the Export Development Corportion become more and more familiar." Sixteen companies received half of the 415 loans to 138 identified companies authorized by the EDC between 1969 and 1980. One of them received 40. One Crown corporation, Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd., which led groups of exporters in negotiations of turnkey projects related to the sale of Candu nuclear reactors, received 25 per cent of all the financing authorized by the EDC during that period. Over-all, six companies received half of the total value of loans authorized by the corporation during those years. Therefore, leaving aside the AEC1, the number of companies that received half the total amount of loans authorized over the period is 19, still a small figure. The report questions, "Could it be that these exporters have not yet reached maturity? One is rather tempted to believe that, for these firms, the subsidy has become a form of permanent assistance."
Last year the EDC lent or facilitated bank financing in the sum of $2.5 billion. Of that amount, $1 billion went to Bombardier, $200,000 went to de Havilland, and $100,000 to Spar Aerospace. Thus, three of the 62 comanies that received EDC financing last year received more than half of the total money.
The EDC has not always conducted transactions that are in the best interests of Canadian taxpayers and their children. The EDC has financed Inco Developments in Indonesia and Guatemala, thus jeopardizing jobs in Sudbury and Manitoba.
The EDC has financed forest development projects in Mexico, Poland and Peru, developments that will compete with Canadian forest products. The EDC helped to finance the construction of a monument to the Algerian revolution. Is that not a high priority?
At a time when Government borrowing costs were in the range of 16 per cent, the EDC arranged a 9.7 per cent loan of $563 million U.S. to assist Bombardier in the sale of subway cars to New York City. Forty per cent of the jobs created by this deal are in the United States.
Often the EDC will be indecisive or will not match a foreign country's offer. A March 29, 1983, Globe and Mail article stated, "A Canadian company has lost a $70 million (U.S.) export order to build an iron foundry in Saudi Arabia because the federally financed Export Development Corporation could not match private European financing terms".
The EDC is supposed to aid Canadian exporters by subsidizing export financing. However, the agency's requirements for financial guarantees from the buyer were so stiff that with the guarantees, Stell Technology Limited of Burlington, Ontario, could have borrowed the money more cheaply from a commercial bank.
